papers.fd: In the new GREG georeferenced dataset of ethnic groups, groups with a single territorial cluster face a significantly higher risk of conflict onset; raising clusters from 1 to the mean 6.86 cuts predicted probability by about 20%.

papers.t: Europe's Tired, Poor, Huddled Masses: Self-Selection and Economic Outcomes in the Age of Mass Migration
papers.af: Ran Abramitzky, Leah Platt Boustan, Katherine Eriksson
papers.ab: During the age of mass migration (1850-1913), one of the largest migration episodes in history, the United States maintained a nearly open border, allowing the study of migrant decisions unhindered by entry restrictions. We estimate the return to migration while accounting for migrant selection by comparing Norway-to-US migrants with their brothers who stayed in Norway in the late nineteenth century. We also compare fathers of migrants and nonmigrants by wealth and occupation. We find that the return to migration was relatively low (70 percent) and that migrants from urban areas were negatively selected from the sending population. "Keep, ancient lands, your storied pomp!" cries she With silent lips. "Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free, The wretched refuse of your teeming shore. Send these, the homeless, tempest-tost to me, I lift my lamp beside the golden door!"--Emma Lazarus (1883).
papers.fd: Norwegian migrants earned about 70% more than brothers who stayed, and urban migrants were negatively selected.

papers.t: Politically Connected Boards of Directors and The Allocation of Procurement Contracts
papers.af: Eitan Goldman, Jörg Rocholl, Jongil So
papers.ab: Abstract This article analyzes whether political connections of the board of directors of publicly traded companies in the USA affect the allocation of government procurement contracts. It focuses on the change in control of both House and Senate following the 1994 election and finds that companies with boards connected to the winning (losing) party experience a significant and large increase (decrease) in procurement contracts after the election. The results remain significant after controlling for industry classifications as well as for several other company characteristics. The findings highlight one of the main avenues through which corporate political connections add value to US companies.
papers.fd: After the 1994 shift of House and Senate control, firms with boards connected to the winning party gained procurement contracts (+$270 million) and those connected to the losing party lost (-$77 million), relative to other firms.

papers.t: High-Dimensional Methods and Inference on Structural and Treatment Effects
papers.af: Alexandre Belloni, Victor Chernozhukov, Christian Hansen
papers.ab: Data with a large number of variables relative to the sample size—“high-dimensional data”—are readily available and increasingly common in empirical economics. Highdimensional data arise through a combination of two phenomena. First, the data may be inherently high dimensional in that many different characteristics per observation are available. For example, the US Census collects information on hundreds of individual characteristics and scanner datasets record transaction-level data for households across a wide range of products. Second, even when the number of available variables is relatively small, researchers rarely know the exact functional form with which the small number of variables enter the model of interest. Researchers are thus faced with a large set of potential variables formed by different ways of interacting and transforming the underlying variables. This paper provides an overview of how innovations in “data mining” can be adapted and modified to provide high-quality inference about model parameters. Note that we use the term “data mining” in a modern sense which denotes a principled search for “true” predictive power that guards against false discovery and overfitting, does not erroneously equate in-sample fit to out-of-sample predictive ability, and accurately accounts for using the same data to examine many different hypotheses or models.

papers.t: Public Attitudes Toward Immigration
papers.ab: Immigrant populations in many developed democracies have grown rapidly, and so too has an extensive literature on natives' attitudes toward immigration. This research has developed from two theoretical foundations, one grounded in political economy, the other in political psychology. These two literatures have developed largely in isolation from one another, yet the conclusions that emerge from each are strikingly similar. Consistently, immigration attitudes show little evidence of being strongly correlated with personal economic circumstances. Instead, research finds that immigration attitudes are shaped by sociotropic concerns about its cultural impacts—and to a lesser extent its economic impacts—on the nation as a whole. This pattern of results has held up as scholars have increasingly turned to experimental tests, and it holds for the United States, Canada, and Western Europe. Still, more work is needed to strengthen the causal identification of sociotropic concerns and to isolate precisely how, when, and why they matter for attitude formation.
papers.fd: Natives' immigration attitudes show little correlation with personal economic circumstances and are shaped instead by sociotropic concerns about national-level cultural and economic impacts (review; CReAM working-paper version).

papers.t: Making Clientelism Work: How Norms of Reciprocity Increase Voter Compliance
papers.af: Chappell H. Lawson, Kenneth F. Greene

papers.t: Poor Institutions, Rich Mines: Resource Curse in the Origins of the Sicilian Mafia
papers.af: Paolo Buonanno, Ruben Durante, Giovanni Prarolo, Paolo Vanin
papers.ab: With weak law-enforcement institutions, a positive shock to the value of natural resources may increase demand for private protection and opportunities for rent appropriation through extortion, favoring the emergence of mafia-type organizations. We test this hypothesis by investigating the emergence of the mafia in XIX century Sicily, where a severe lack of state property-right enforcement coincided with a steep rise in international demand for sulfur, Sicily's most valuable export commodity. Using historical data on the early incidence of mafia activity and on the distribution of sulfur reserves, we document that the mafia was more present in municipalities with greater sulfur availability.
papers.fd: Mafia emerged in 19th-century Sicilian towns with more sulfur, a resource boom under weak property-rights enforcement.

papers.t: Social Incentives in Organizations
papers.ab: We review the evidence on social incentives, namely on how social interactions with colleagues, subordinates, bosses, customers, and others shape agents’ effort choices in organizations. We propose a two-way taxonomy based on ( a) whether the social group is horizontal (peers at the same level of the hierarchy) or vertical (individuals at different levels within or outside of the organization) and ( b) whether the agent's effort creates externalities for the other members of their social group. We show settings in which social incentives improve productivity and settings in which they reduce it. In most cases, the size of the effect is approximately 10%, which is half of the typical effect of performance pay. We also show that social incentives can interfere with financial incentives, making them ineffective or even detrimental. We conclude that social incentives are a powerful motivator that must be taken into account in the design of organizational policies and that more research is needed to understand how policies can shape the preferences that underpin these incentives.
papers.fd: Social incentives move effort by about 10%, half of typical performance-pay effects, and can clash with financial incentives.

papers.t: Channeling Fisher: Randomization Tests and the Statistical Insignificance of Seemingly Significant Experimental Results*
papers.ab: I follow R. A. Fisher's,The Design of Experiments (1935), using randomization statistical inference to test the null hypothesis of no treatment effects in a comprehensive sample of 53 experimental papers drawn from the journals of the American Economic Association. In the average paper, randomization tests of the significance of individual treatment effects find 13% to 22% fewer significant results than are found using authors’ methods. In joint tests of multiple treatment effects appearing together in tables, randomization tests yield 33% to 49% fewer statistically significant results than conventional tests. Bootstrap and jackknife methods support and confirm the randomization results.

branches.name: Institutions, history & persistence
branches.desc: Why some societies have inclusive institutions; long shadows of colonialism, land, and early states.
branches.narrative: The colonial-origins programme (Acemoglu, Johnson & Robinson 2001; Dell 2010; Nunn 2008) is now the canon every course opens with. The frontier has moved from whether institutions matter to how specific historical arrangements — forced labour, indirect rule, concessions, early state presence — travel into today's state capacity, trust and beliefs. The 2026 syllabi pair these shocks with anthropology on lineage, religion and kinship, and with theory of why inefficient institutions persist.

branches.name: Democracy, regimes & political transitions
branches.desc: Franchise, democratization, autocracy, populism; what regime change does to growth and public goods.
branches.narrative: Acemoglu–Robinson's commitment theory of transitions is the backbone; Acemoglu, Naidu, Restrepo & Robinson (2019) closed much of the cross-country growth debate. The frontier is micro: what democracy actually delivers (access more than quality: Kudamatsu, Harding, Martinez-Bravo et al.), how autocracies govern and censor (China's cadre system, village elections, information control), and why voters turn to populists after trade, austerity and financial shocks.

branches.name: Voters, elections & accountability
branches.desc: Do elections discipline and select? Information, attribution, budget cycles and distributive politics.
branches.narrative: The empirics of political agency — random audits and re-election incentives in Brazil (Ferraz & Finan 2008, 2011) — are the most-taught papers in the atlas. The frontier asks when information actually moves voters (news relative to priors), why voters punish malfeasance more than they reward quality, how attribution breaks across tiers of government, and how electoral incentives distort the location and visibility of spending, now measured with granular administrative data.

branches.name: Politicians: selection, representation & identity
branches.desc: Who governs matters: quotas, quality, pay, dynasties and the returns to office.
branches.narrative: Quota experiments (Chattopadhyay & Duflo 2004; Pande 2003) established that the identity of office-holders changes policy. The frontier is political selection: who runs and why (Dal Bó et al. 2017), quotas and the 'mediocre man', experiments in candidate selection and candidate training, party gatekeeping against women, and new outcomes — environment, health, welfare delivery — through which representation shows up.

branches.name: Clientelism, patronage & electoral malpractice
branches.desc: Votes for particularistic benefits, jobs for supporters, fraud and violence — and what weakens them.
branches.narrative: A first generation documented vote buying and its enforcement (Wantchekon 2003; Finan & Schechter 2012; Stokes). A second opened up brokers and networks. The current frontier asks what weakens clientelism — reducing voters' material dependence works more reliably than information — and measures patronage inside bureaucracies with personnel records, showing who gets hired and what it costs in service quality.

branches.name: Corruption & political connections
branches.desc: Measuring graft, the value of connections, and anti-corruption policy.
branches.narrative: Measurement papers (Olken 2007; Fisman 2001; Khwaja & Mian 2005; Olken & Barron 2009) built the field. The frontier moves to the long-run effects of anti-corruption policy (audits), procurement microdata, and the general-equilibrium costs of connections for firms and misallocation.

branches.name: State capacity, bureaucracy & implementation
branches.desc: Fiscal and legal capacity, bureaucrats' selection and incentives, frontline delivery, decentralization and oversight.
branches.narrative: Besley & Persson's state-capacity framework gave the macro logic; a personnel-economics-of-the-state boom supplied the micro evidence on selecting, paying, posting and managing bureaucrats. The frontier reconnects bureaucracy to politics: whether bureaucratic quality mediates electoral accountability, how patronage and autonomy interact, and how low-capacity states raise taxes and deliver services.

branches.name: Interest groups, lobbying & money in politics
branches.desc: Organized interests, contributions, revolving doors and the diffuse-benefit problem.
branches.narrative: Lobbying research moved from Grossman–Helpman theory to firm-level disclosure data on connections versus expertise, hidden channels such as corporate philanthropy, campaign-finance limits, and organisations that trade votes for public funding. The diffuse-benefit, concentrated-cost problem at the heart of reform is still mostly theoretical — an opening for new evidence.

branches.name: Media, information & persuasion
branches.desc: News markets, bias, persuasion, propaganda, social media and censorship.
branches.narrative: Media economics began with accountability (Besley & Burgess 2002; Strömberg 2004; Snyder & Strömberg 2010) and bias (Gentzkow & Shapiro). The frontier is persuasion and polarisation on cable, social media and messaging apps, misinformation, the decline of local news, and how autocrats manage information without overt repression.

branches.name: Conflict, violence & crime
branches.desc: Civil war, insurgency, organized crime, repression and protest.
branches.narrative: Income shocks and civil conflict (Miguel, Satyanath & Sergenti 2004; Dube & Vargas 2013) and counterinsurgency are the canon. The frontier has turned to crime and criminal governance — gangs, mafias and cartels as rivals to the state — to the legacies of violence, and to protest and collective action under authoritarian rule.

branches.name: Culture, identity & political preferences
branches.desc: Trust and norms, diversity, beliefs about redistribution, nation-building and economic shocks to preferences.
branches.narrative: Culture entered political economy through trust and values (Tabellini; Guiso, Sapienza & Zingales; Nunn & Wantchekon). The 2026 syllabi push into kinship, morality and cultural evolution, nation-building and identity, and the political consequences of trade, automation and immigration shocks.

branches.name: Policy-making: legislatures, parties, fiscal & international politics
branches.desc: Positive political theory of policy: redistribution, bargaining, parties, constitutions and IPE.
branches.narrative: The workhorse theory — median voter, probabilistic voting, legislative bargaining, citizen candidates, constitutions — still anchors every PhD course. The empirical frontier estimates these models with roll calls, text and structural methods, studies polarisation and partisanship in firms and markets, and brings geopolitics and economic coercion into international political economy.

branches.name: Methods & adjacent development economics
branches.desc: Econometric toolkits and non-political development topics that appear in the syllabi (kept for completeness, hidden by default).

leaves.name: Colonial origins & extractive institutions
leaves.settled: Extractive colonial institutions have persistent effects on income, public goods and trust (mita, slave trades, land tenure, forced cultivation).
leaves.open: Which channels carry persistence — state presence, missions, local elites, beliefs — and when colonial legacies reverse.

leaves.name: Persistence, culture & historical legacies
leaves.settled: Historical shocks leave measurable traces in today's outcomes and beliefs.
leaves.open: Separating true persistence from spatial noise; observing the mechanism in intermediate periods rather than only at the endpoints.

leaves.name: State formation & historical state capacity
leaves.settled: Early state formation, war and urban autonomy shaped fiscal capacity and representation in Europe and China.
leaves.open: State formation outside Europe and the role of local intermediaries (chiefs, lineages) in building capacity.

leaves.name: Theory of (inefficient) institutions & elites
leaves.settled: Inefficient institutions persist because changing them threatens the power of those who benefit (no political Coase theorem).
leaves.open: How reforms that shift de facto power become self-sustaining; the corridor between despotic and absent states.

leaves.name: Land, property rights & rural elites
leaves.settled: Land and labour arrangements anchor rural elite power; secret ballots and land reforms shift it.
leaves.open: Distributional and political effects of titling and land reform at scale; agrarian elites and structural transformation.

leaves.name: Franchise extension & democratization theory
leaves.settled: Franchise extensions respond to revolutionary threats and to elites' calculations about public goods.
leaves.open: Transitions triggered by autocrats' errors; how enfranchisement becomes effective representation.

leaves.name: Democracy, growth & redistribution
leaves.settled: Democracy raises growth in the long run, through reforms, schooling and health.
leaves.open: Which democratic institutions do the work, and how delivering growth sustains support for democracy.

leaves.name: Democracy & access to public services
leaves.settled: Democracy expands access to schooling, health and electricity more than it improves quality.
leaves.open: Why the quality gap persists under democracy: the core puzzle of the VoxDevLit review.

leaves.name: Autocracy, China & authoritarian politics
leaves.settled: Autocracies govern through cadre evaluation, controlled local elections, co-optation and repression.
leaves.open: Information management, AI-enabled surveillance and the limits of top-down accountability.

leaves.name: Populism, polarization & democratic backsliding
leaves.settled: Trade shocks, austerity and financial crises raise support for populist and radical-right parties; populist rule lowers growth.
leaves.open: Demand versus supply of populism; identity and status; what makes democracies resist backsliding.

leaves.name: Voting behavior, turnout & electoral rules
leaves.settled: Turnout responds to costs, social pressure and habit; electoral rules shape strategic voting.
leaves.open: Structural estimates of voter behaviour; policy effects of new voting rules (ranked choice, vote by mail).

leaves.name: Enfranchisement & who votes
leaves.settled: Enfranchising poorer or excluded voters shifts spending toward them (electronic voting in Brazil; the Voting Rights Act).
leaves.open: Whether voter-ID and registration rules change turnout and outcomes; enfranchisement where the state is weak.

leaves.name: Electoral incentives & political agency (discipline)
leaves.settled: Re-election incentives reduce corruption and raise effort; term limits change behaviour.
leaves.open: When electoral incentives distort rather than discipline, and how bureaucratic quality mediates them.

leaves.name: Information, transparency & retrospective voting
leaves.settled: Credible information about malfeasance moves votes, especially through local media.
leaves.open: News relative to priors; information versus vote buying; information under polarisation and misinformation.

leaves.name: Do voters reward delivery? Visibility & attribution
leaves.settled: Visible, attributable benefits (cash, roads, housing) are rewarded; quality improvements often are not.
leaves.open: Why quality goes unrewarded (observability, attribution across tiers, time horizons) and designs that make quality legible.

leaves.name: Distributive politics, targeting & budget cycles
leaves.settled: Governments target spending to aligned and swing areas and time it to elections.
leaves.open: The welfare cost of political targeting measured with administrative microdata; enforcement and forbearance as targeting.

leaves.name: Ethnic politics, favoritism & identity voting
leaves.settled: Co-ethnic favouritism is widespread and falls under democracy; information can weaken identity voting.
leaves.open: When favouritism is feasible (segregation) and how polarisation changes it.

leaves.name: Political selection & politician quality
leaves.settled: Pay, entry costs and party gatekeeping shape who runs and how competent they are.
leaves.open: Experiments in candidate recruitment, selection and training; motivations for candidacy.

leaves.name: Descriptive representation: gender, caste, minorities
leaves.settled: Reserved seats for women, castes and tribes shift policy toward their priorities.
leaves.open: New outcomes (environment, health, welfare delivery) and why some quotas deliver little.

leaves.name: Leaders, dynasties & political families
leaves.settled: Leaders matter for growth and institutions; political families persist.
leaves.open: Dynasties' effects on development and selection; leader age, education and experience.

leaves.name: Returns to office & politicians' private interests
leaves.settled: Office brings private returns, larger where oversight is weak.
leaves.open: Insider trading and post-office careers as distortions of policy.

leaves.name: Citizen-candidate & entry models
leaves.settled: When politicians cannot commit, the identity of whoever is elected sets policy.
leaves.open: Structural citizen-candidate models of entry.

leaves.name: Clientelism & vote buying
leaves.settled: Vote buying persists under the secret ballot through reciprocity, brokers and monitoring.
leaves.open: What breaks clientelist equilibria: reducing dependence, audits, programmatic outsiders.

leaves.name: Patronage in public employment
leaves.settled: Patronage hiring selects less competent staff and lowers service quality, though appointees can still be held accountable.
leaves.open: Combining patronage and merit; when political control of bureaucrats helps delivery.

leaves.name: Electoral fraud, violence & coercion
leaves.settled: Fraud, intimidation and violence are electoral tools of the strong; simple monitoring reduces fraud.
leaves.open: Electoral violence by armed groups and gangs; technology for election integrity.

leaves.name: Reducing clientelism & dependence
leaves.settled: Reducing material vulnerability weakens clientelism more reliably than information.
leaves.open: Durability of de-clientelisation and politicians' counter-strategies.

leaves.name: Measuring corruption & anti-corruption policy
leaves.settled: Corruption can be measured (missing funds, bribes, audits) and responds to monitoring and penalties.
leaves.open: Long-run and general-equilibrium effects of anti-corruption policy; procurement design.

leaves.name: Political connections & rents for firms
leaves.settled: Connected firms earn rents through credit, contracts and regulation.
leaves.open: Economy-wide misallocation costs and the political demand side of connections.

leaves.name: Theory of corruption & misgovernance
leaves.settled: The structure of corruption (independent versus joint monopolies) and officials' incentives determine bribe levels.
leaves.open: Theory linking corruption to state capacity and information.

leaves.name: State capacity & fiscal capacity (theory, macro)
leaves.settled: Fiscal and legal capacity are investments made when common interests and cohesive institutions prevail.
leaves.open: Norms of reciprocity and civic culture as complements to institutions; measuring capacity.

leaves.name: Taxation, tax compliance & revenue
leaves.settled: Third-party reporting, enforcement and collector incentives raise revenue in low-capacity states.
leaves.open: Taxation as a channel of citizen engagement; the tax-service link; administrative capacity ceilings.

leaves.name: Bureaucrats: selection, incentives & allocation
leaves.settled: Selection, pay, postings and autonomy change bureaucratic performance.
leaves.open: Bureaucracy inside politics: alignment, ideology and patronage within the state.

leaves.name: Frontline service delivery & absenteeism
leaves.settled: Frontline absence and low quality are pervasive; monitoring helps, but reforms are often rolled back.
leaves.open: The political feasibility of frontline reforms and the role of unions.

leaves.name: Decentralization & local government
leaves.settled: Decentralisation trades local information against capture; smaller units can improve delivery.
leaves.open: Government splits and amalgamations; local capacity as the condition for gains.

leaves.name: Oversight, audits, courts & checks
leaves.settled: Checks and audits deter malfeasance, but controllers face the same political failures.
leaves.open: Oversight that does not become a bottleneck; courts and audit bodies.

leaves.name: Lobbying & special-interest influence
leaves.settled: Lobbying buys both access (connections) and expertise; organised industries obtain favourable policy.
leaves.open: Hidden channels (philanthropy, foreign influence) and lobbying's misallocation costs.

leaves.name: Campaign finance & contributions
leaves.settled: Money has modest effects on vote shares; spending limits change competition.
leaves.open: Campaign-finance reform effects on entry and incumbency; donor influence on enforcement.

leaves.name: Collective action & concentrated vs diffuse interests
leaves.settled: Concentrated groups organise; diffuse beneficiaries rarely do.
leaves.open: When diffuse interests organise: the central gap for the reform agenda.

leaves.name: Regulation & regulatory capture
leaves.settled: Regulators respond to industry and political pressure; revolving doors exist.
leaves.open: Discretion versus rules in enforcement; capture in environmental and financial regulation.

leaves.name: Media & political accountability
leaves.settled: Media coverage raises government responsiveness and political knowledge.
leaves.open: The decline of local news and the nationalisation of politics.

leaves.name: Media bias & slant
leaves.settled: Slant follows audience demand more than owners' preferences.
leaves.open: Measuring bias with text; competition and truth.

leaves.name: Persuasion, propaganda & media capture
leaves.settled: Media and propaganda persuade, from radio to cable television.
leaves.open: Persistence of persuasion and polarisation; narratives.

leaves.name: Internet, social media & misinformation
leaves.settled: Internet and social media change participation, protest and polarisation.
leaves.open: Platform design, misinformation and politicians' online behaviour.

leaves.name: Censorship & information control
leaves.settled: Autocrats censor strategically and allow some freedom when it is useful to them.
leaves.open: Informational autocracy and AI-driven control.

leaves.name: Theories of conflict & bargaining failure
leaves.settled: Wars follow commitment and information problems.
leaves.open: Bargaining models estimated with data on coalitions and insurgencies.

leaves.name: Economic shocks & civil conflict
leaves.settled: Income shocks change conflict through opportunity costs and the value of the prize.
leaves.open: Climate, migration and pastoralism as conflict drivers.

leaves.name: Counterinsurgency, aid & state-building in war
leaves.settled: Aid and counterinsurgency can win or lose hearts and minds depending on design.
leaves.open: Long-run state-building effects of interventions.

leaves.name: Ethnic conflict, genocide & mass violence
leaves.settled: Propaganda and polarisation drive mass violence.
leaves.open: Cultural distance and the micro-dynamics of atrocities.

leaves.name: Organized crime, gangs & politics
leaves.settled: Organised crime captures politics and provides governance where the state is absent.
leaves.open: Criminal governance, gangs and state responses.

leaves.name: Protest, revolution & collective action
leaves.settled: Protests are strategic and can shift elites, opinion and votes.
leaves.open: When protests change policy and when they provoke backlash.

leaves.name: Consequences of conflict & repression
leaves.settled: Violence leaves lasting political, economic and psychological legacies.
leaves.open: Repression's effects on loyalty and opposition.

leaves.name: Culture, trust & social capital
leaves.settled: Culture and trust shape institutions and development and are shaped by them.
leaves.open: Morality, kinship and cultural evolution as foundations of political behaviour.

leaves.name: Ethnic diversity, fractionalization & public goods
leaves.settled: Diversity can lower public-goods provision through weaker sanctions and divergent preferences.
leaves.open: Intergroup contact and nation-building as remedies.

leaves.name: Preferences for redistribution & beliefs
leaves.settled: Beliefs about mobility and fairness drive support for redistribution.
leaves.open: How malleable these beliefs are, and how they interact with immigration.

leaves.name: Nation-building, identity & schooling
leaves.settled: States build identity through schooling, language and propaganda.
leaves.open: Discrimination by street-level bureaucrats and identity politics.

leaves.name: Trade, migration & economic shocks to politics
leaves.settled: Trade, automation and immigration shocks shift votes toward nationalists.
leaves.open: Status and cultural channels versus economic losses.

leaves.name: Redistribution & the size of government
leaves.settled: Redistribution follows the median voter only loosely; inequality and institutions mediate.
leaves.open: Inequality and political power; preferences versus institutions.

leaves.name: Legislatures, bargaining & agenda setting
leaves.settled: Agenda power and bargaining rules shape distribution in legislatures.
leaves.open: Structural estimation of legislative bargaining and committees.

leaves.name: Parties, ideology & polarization
leaves.settled: Parties matter for policy, and polarisation has risen.
leaves.open: Polarisation in firms and markets; affective polarisation.

leaves.name: Constitutions, political institutions & policy
leaves.settled: Electoral rules and forms of government change fiscal outcomes.
leaves.open: Credible quasi-experimental tests of constitutional effects.

leaves.name: Macro political economy & fiscal policy
leaves.settled: Delayed stabilisation and budget cycles stem from distributional conflict.
leaves.open: Fiscal rules and their enforcement.

leaves.name: International political economy & geopolitics
leaves.settled: Trade policy reflects organised interests and electoral geography.
leaves.open: Geopolitics, economic coercion and fragmentation.

leaves.name: Adjacent development micro (health, education, credit, labor)

mechs.name: Median voter & redistribution
mechs.architecture: Parties compete for voters (Downs)
mechs.logic: With majority rule over a single redistributive tax, policy is set by the median voter; the further the median falls below mean income, the more redistribution.
predictions: Extending the franchise to poorer voters raises spending/redistribution
Higher inequality (mean/median) raises redistribution

mechs.name: Probabilistic voting & swing-voter targeting
mechs.architecture: Parties compete for voters (probabilistic voting)
mechs.logic: When voters have idiosyncratic ideological attachment, parties target transfers to groups with many swing (ideologically moderate, responsive) voters — or to core voters if they have a delivery advantage.
predictions: Spending flows to swing/contested districts (or aligned core areas)
Groups with more responsive voters receive more

mechs.name: Electoral discipline (moral hazard)
mechs.architecture: Voters discipline incumbents (Ferejohn)
mechs.logic: Voters set a retrospective performance threshold for re-election; incumbents who value office restrain rents/exert effort to meet it. The discipline vanishes when re-election is impossible.
predictions: Term-limited (lame-duck) incumbents steal more / exert less effort
Discipline stronger when voters observe performance

mechs.name: Electoral selection of types (adverse selection)
mechs.architecture: Voters select politician types (Fearon)
mechs.logic: Elections screen good types; voters use performance signals to update about competence/honesty and retain good types. Information quality determines how well elections select.
predictions: Information about performance changes re-election odds in the direction of the news relative to priors
Re-elected politicians are positively selected

mechs.name: Career concerns, pandering & signaling
mechs.architecture: Informed actors signal to voters
mechs.logic: Office-holders distort policy toward what voters can observe or believe is right in order to signal competence; pre-electoral cycles in visible spending arise from competence signaling.
predictions: Pre-election shifts toward visible/attributable spending
Stronger distortions where voters are less informed or democracy is young

mechs.name: Visibility & attribution bias (credit claiming)
mechs.architecture: Voters reward what they can observe and attribute
mechs.logic: Because voters observe and attribute some outputs (roads, transfers) better than others (learning, clinical quality, maintenance), electoral competition over-supplies visible goods and under-supplies quality.
predictions: Visible goods are electorally rewarded; quality improvements are not
Shared responsibility across tiers weakens reward

mechs.name: Citizen-candidates: who governs matters
mechs.architecture: Citizens decide whether to run (Osborne–Slivinski / Besley–Coate)
mechs.logic: Politicians cannot commit to platforms; policy reflects the identity/preferences of whoever is elected, so rules shaping who runs and wins (quotas, pay, entry costs) change policy.
predictions: Mandated representation (gender, caste) shifts policy toward the group's priorities
Higher pay or lower entry costs change politician quality

mechs.name: Commitment problems & de facto power
mechs.architecture: Promises that cannot be made credible (Acemoglu–Robinson)
mechs.logic: Elites cannot credibly promise future redistribution, so they concede institutions (franchise) under threat of revolution; inefficient institutions persist because the powerful fear losing de facto power (political replacement effect).
predictions: Franchise extensions follow revolutionary threats
Elites block growth-enhancing changes that erode their power
De facto power persists even after de jure reform

mechs.name: Legislative bargaining & agenda power
mechs.architecture: Politicians divide a surplus (Baron–Ferejohn)
mechs.logic: Proposal power yields a disproportionate share of the surplus; minimal winning coalitions form; procedural rules shape distribution.
predictions: Agenda setters' districts receive more
Universalism vs minimal coalitions depending on rules

mechs.name: Rent-seeking contests & conflict technology
mechs.architecture: Groups expend resources to win (Tullock)
mechs.logic: When prizes are contested, groups invest in unproductive appropriation; the size of rents and the contest technology determine resources wasted.
predictions: Bigger contestable rents raise lobbying/fighting effort

mechs.name: Lobbying & common agency (protection for sale)
mechs.architecture: Organized groups buy influence via contributions or information
mechs.logic: Organized groups offer contribution schedules (or information/access) to policymakers who weigh welfare against contributions; organized sectors get policies favorable to them.
predictions: Organized industries receive more protection/favorable regulation
Connections and expertise both carry value

mechs.name: Collective action & concentrated vs diffuse interests
mechs.architecture: Small groups with concentrated stakes organize; large diffuse groups free-ride
mechs.logic: Concentrated losers from reform organize more effectively than diffuse winners, so welfare-improving reforms with diffuse benefits are blocked or reversed.
predictions: Reforms hurting organized providers (unions, incumbents) are weakened or reversed
Beneficiaries' mobilization is rare without organizational vehicles

mechs.name: Clientelism as conditional exchange
mechs.architecture: Credible conditional exchange of private benefits for votes
mechs.logic: Where programmatic promises lack credibility, politicians use targetable, contingent benefits (cash, jobs) enforced by brokers/monitoring; poorer, more dependent voters are cheaper to buy.
predictions: Reducing material dependence weakens clientelism
Patronage jobs inflate low-productivity public employment
Vote buying persists despite secret ballot via reciprocity/monitoring

mechs.name: Politics of fear & identity loyalty
mechs.architecture: Group loyalty as equilibrium outcome
mechs.logic: Citizens tolerate bad co-ethnic leaders because replacing them risks the other group taking power; this political slack lets leaders extract rents.
predictions: Favoritism and rents higher where group power is contested
Institutions that allow within-group replacement (reservations) raise governance

mechs.name: Coordinating punishment & self-enforcing constraints
mechs.architecture: Citizens must coordinate punishment (Weingast)
mechs.logic: Limits on rulers are self-enforcing only if citizens can coordinate to punish transgressions; focal rules, information and elections act as coordination devices.
predictions: Shared signals (elections, protests, media) enable coordinated sanctions
Divided citizens permit transgressions

mechs.name: Strategic information transmission
mechs.architecture: Informed actors communicate strategically (Crawford–Sobel)
mechs.logic: Senders with misaligned preferences can only convey coarse information; credibility depends on alignment. Applies to lobbyists, bureaucrats, experts, media.
predictions: Information value falls with preference misalignment
Delegation to aligned experts dominates

mechs.name: Media markets, bias & capture
mechs.architecture: Market for news shapes what voters know
mechs.logic: Media coverage informs voters, raising politicians' responsiveness to covered groups; bias arises from demand (reader priors) or supply (owners, government capture), and captured media weakens accountability.
predictions: Coverage raises responsiveness/spending toward audiences
Slant follows readers' ideology
Captured media sustains incumbents

mechs.name: State capacity as investment (clusters of prosperity)
mechs.architecture: Forward-looking investment in fiscal/legal capacity
mechs.logic: Governments invest in fiscal and legal capacity when they expect to reap benefits and face common-interest pressures (external war, cohesive institutions); political instability and polarization reduce investment; civic norms complement institutions.
predictions: Common-interest threats (war) raise fiscal capacity
Cohesive institutions/executive constraints raise capacity
Weak states cluster with violence and low income

mechs.name: Bureaucratic principal-agent (selection & incentives)
mechs.architecture: Citizens → politicians → bureaucrats chain of agency
mechs.logic: Bureaucrats respond to pay, career incentives and mission; multitasking makes high-powered incentives risky; selection on motivation matters; authority allocation trades off loss of control vs agent information.
predictions: Performance pay raises measured output (and possibly bribes)
Higher wages attract more able applicants without lowering motivation
Autonomy helps when monitors are the bottleneck

mechs.name: Local capture vs local information (decentralization)
mechs.architecture: Trade-off between information/accountability and elite capture
mechs.logic: Lower-level governments know local preferences and are easier to monitor, but are more prone to capture by local elites, especially where inequality is high and voters are uninformed.
predictions: Decentralization improves allocation where local capacity is high and capture low
Targeting worsens in unequal localities

mechs.name: Corruption, extortion & the industrial organization of bribes
mechs.architecture: Officials price bureaucratic goods; market structure of bribe-takers matters
mechs.logic: Bribe levels depend on the structure of the corruption network (independent vs joint monopolies), the probability of detection and officials' outside options.
predictions: Monitoring/audits reduce theft
Higher official wages or detection probabilities reduce bribes
Uncoordinated multiple officials extract more

mechs.name: Bargaining failure & the opportunity cost of conflict
mechs.architecture: Commitment and information problems make costly war rational
mechs.logic: Wars occur when parties cannot commit or have private information; income shocks change the opportunity cost of fighting (labor-intensive goods) vs the value of the prize (capital-intensive/natural resources).
predictions: Labor-intensive price shocks reduce conflict; resource price shocks raise it
Rapid power shifts trigger preventive war

mechs.name: Cultural transmission & co-evolution with institutions
mechs.architecture: Values transmitted vertically/horizontally; interact with institutions
mechs.logic: Cultural traits (trust, cooperation norms) are transmitted across generations and respond to institutions; good institutions raise the fitness of civic values, creating multipliers and persistence.
predictions: Historical shocks leave persistent effects on trust/values
Institutions and culture are complements

mechs.name: Diversity, preferences & public goods
mechs.architecture: Heterogeneous preferences / weaker sanctions reduce public-good provision
mechs.logic: Ethnic heterogeneity lowers public-good provision via divergent preferences, weaker cross-group social sanctions, or lower altruism; polarization raises conflict.
predictions: More fractionalized localities provide fewer public goods
Polarization predicts conflict more than fractionalization

contested.label: stock, returns, firms, abnormal
contested.why: Event studies mostly find ties raise firm value; C00019 is negative only because its event was bad news for Suharto (implying positive value), leaving the Cheney null (C00197) and the Malaysian crisis loss (W3122513589) as genuine but event-specific dissent.

contested.label: vote, party, incumbent, turnout
contested.why: Same relationship, no framing problem: five studies find benefits raise incumbent support, Uganda grants (C01138) and NREGS exposure (C01241) find the reverse, and C00460 finds Progresa's earlier positive result was a data-merge error, contradicting C00226.

contested.label: vote, elections, polling, station
contested.why: Same relationship (roads, electrification, services and incumbent vote), no framing issue: four studies find a reward, C01172 finds better services cut ANC support, and C00663 finds PMGSY roads had no effect, contradicting C00656 on the same programme.

contested.label: growth, capita, outcomes, income
contested.why: Same relationship (democracy and growth) with democracy the cause in every card: within-country transition studies find faster growth while Barro finds a weakly negative effect and Przeworski et al. none, the classic cross-section versus panel split.

contested.label: elections, vote, municipality, national
contested.why: Same relationship (local migrant or refugee presence and far-right vote), same framing of the cause: three studies of large or sudden inflows find gains while C02108 finds a small reception centre cut Front National growth, a genuine conflict that fits contact theory.

contested.label: infant, first, death, child
contested.why: C01199 is signed on school attendance (which rose) although its infant-death estimate is negative like C00336, so on infant mortality the two agree once flipped; the genuine dispute left is C01908, which finds democracy has little or no effect on infant and child mortality.

thin.why: The paper would link civil-service reform or randomly assigned senior bureaucrats to local income and nightlights; the field has measured state capacity and service quality (23 papers) but almost never the final development payoff.

The paper would treat bureaucrats as inputs to firms, using inspector, licensing-officer or procurement-official reassignments and civil-service rule changes against firm entry, investment and productivity in administrative data.

The paper would test the fiscal contract at scale: does being taxed (property-tax enforcement, withholding versus lump-sum payment) change whether citizens punish incumbents, turn out or demand services? The one design that exists is coded as civic participation.

The paper would show how local economic shocks (trade, commodity, recessions) change who runs and who wins, such as outsiders, populists, women or business candidates, using candidate rosters and shift-share shocks; the supply side of populism is thinly studied.

Enfranchisement studies measure what governments then spend; the paper would follow the newly enfranchised themselves (women, VRA-era Black voters, young and migrant voters) to see whether turnout habits and party alignment persist.

The paper would use discontinuities in electoral design (runoff thresholds, term limits, district magnitude) to test whether better accountability shows up in local income or nightlights, not just in spending, where the evidence already sits.

The paper would use reform adoptions (ranked-choice voting, compulsory voting, PR switches) with panel surveys to test whether electoral design shifts trust, tolerance and policy views; the nearest evidence is compulsory voting shifting policy preferences.

The paper would test whether re-election eligibility and electoral format shape political violence, crime and protest, for example term-limit discontinuities against police and criminal violence in Latin American municipalities.

The paper would trace how local violence or insurgency reallocates public budgets (security versus social spending, which areas are targeted); the war-and-taxes literature covers revenue (taxation and redistribution cells) but not the spending side.

The paper would use an epidemiological design (immigrants or diplomats from high- and low-corruption cultures facing the same rules) to separate cultural transmission of corruption norms from institutions; the Fisman-Miguel parking study is the template.

The paper would test whether disclosing candidates' criminal records or violence-prone networks reduces electoral violence and intimidation; the Nigerian anti-violence campaign is the only paper in this cell.

The paper would ask who earns electoral credit for donor-funded projects (recipient incumbents or donors) using aid-eligibility cutoffs or aid-timing shocks; the Philippine credit-claiming study is the only paper in this cell, and the cash-transfer voting results do not cover donor channels.

The paper would study the voter side of quotas and reservations: turnout of the targeted group, vote choice after exposure to a reserved-seat leader, and whether party vote share falls or rises; only a Spanish list-quota study sits here.

The paper would test whether cultural norms (gender, caste, immigrant background) screen who is nominated and elected, by comparing party gatekeepers with voters using candidate rosters and norm shocks; the Indian caste-equilibrium and Swedish nomination papers are the starting points.

The paper would test whether extending the vote defuses domestic violence beyond the single US Voting Rights Act result, using other enfranchisements (women's suffrage, voting-age cuts, democratisation waves) and event-level violence data; the dyadic democratic-peace card is a different question.

The paper would study how personnel rules for police and soldiers (pay, promotion quotas, rotation, civil-service protection) change crime and state violence, building on the Colombian false-positives and Chinese exam-abolition cases.

The paper would measure discrimination in service delivery at scale with administrative response times and approvals rather than email audits, and test which institutional fixes remove it; the two audit studies here are small and US-only.

The paper would ask whether commodity busts and crises build or erode state capacity, using local exposure to price shocks against bureaucrat headcounts, tax collection and cadastres (the Mexican Depression and Congo coltan papers are the template).

The paper would use electoral-design discontinuities or term-limit changes against firm entry, investment and procurement contracts, testing whether political accountability reaches the private sector; the mechanism is indirect, so the pull is modest.
