Taxes on mobile factors should be centralized to avoid a race to the bottom, so vertical transfers to local governments are needed
Centralized development strategies of the 1950s and 60s produced corruption, absenteeism and poorly targeted policy, prompting the push to devolve responsibilities (World Bank 2004)
contested: Whether centralized provision is uniform and efficient, or distorted by bargaining among district legislators who ignore spillovers (Besley and Coate 2003; Lockwood 2002)
Whether decentralization with local democracy can discipline errant service providers where centralized systems cannot use local performance information (Cremer et al. 1995; Seabright 1996)
Whether central governments truly cannot differentiate local public goods across communities, an assumption of first-generation theory that is not spelled out
gaps: Political distortions in decentralized government beyond capture and corruption
Effects of decentralization on intercommunity allocations, learning and experimentation
Effects of decentralization on democracy itself
How decentralization compares with other organizational alternatives
Design and implementation issues: interjurisdictional spillovers, vertical fiscal relations, the range of devolution and the political economy of implementation
2505.scope: overview focused on developing-country decentralization; overlaps partially with Bardhan (2002) and Bardhan and Mookherjee (2015); slices omit the empirical section and conclusion

2507.claim: Philippine mayors whose municipalities got a World Bank KALAHI-CIDSS project were more likely to be reelected (odds ratio 1.69; 59% to 71%) by claiming credit they did not deserve, even before funds were disbursed.
2507.treatment_desc: participation of a municipality in the World Bank-funded KALAHI-CIDSS community-driven development project, designed to prevent political capture of funds
2507.outcome_desc: reelection of the incumbent mayor (binary); also count of mayoral visits to project-site villages as the credit-claiming mechanism

magnitudes.outcome: odds of incumbent mayor reelection, KALAHI vs non-KALAHI municipalities
reelection probability of incumbent mayor, from 59% to 71%

setting.unit_desc: Philippine municipalities, 155 of them KALAHI-CIDSS recipients, among the poorest 25% in each province

identification.variation: KALAHI sites chosen among the poorest 25% of municipalities in each province by a formula devised outside the World Bank, so mayors could not influence selection; comparison with eligible but yet unfunded municipalities
identification.threat: gains could come from fiscal manipulation or diversion of funds or from deserved credit; tested using municipalities where the project was announced before any funds were disbursed

mechanisms.note: mayors increased visits to project sites and ribbon-cutting; reelection effect appears before disbursement, consistent with voters misattributing the project to the mayor

settled: Foreign aid and domestic politics are highly interrelated: donors pursue strategic goals and recipient politicians divert aid for political ends
Electoral effects of events outside the incumbent's control depend on whether citizens attribute them to the government (Achen and Bartels 2004)
Constituents misattribute credit even in high-information settings, and US legislators claim credit for spending they had little role in securing (Johns 2011; Grimmer et al. 2014)
contested: Whether aid strengthens democratic processes in developing countries, as recent research suggests (Brown et al. 2008; Gugerty and Kremer 2008), or undermines them when incumbents win undeserved credit
Whether the electoral payoff of aid comes from fiscal manipulation of aid or budgets or from undeserved credit claiming
gaps: How widespread undeserved credit claiming is beyond the Philippines, where evidence from Sierra Leone, Uganda and Iraq is only qualitative
Which conditions lead politicians to choose fiscal manipulation versus credit claiming, and what project designs would follow
Whether credit claiming can improve aid outcomes by securing local politicians' support, so donors might let them share credit
Whether credit claiming is greater for nationally allocated aid, where strategic interests may play a larger role
2507.data_asset: KALAHI-CIDSS project and impact-evaluation survey data (including mayoral visits to villages) matched to municipal election outcomes, plus interviews with local politicians and World Bank officials
2507.scope: local-level aid in poor, low-information, clientelistic settings in a project designed to limit capture; reelection not affected by municipal population, economic well-being, land area or urbanization

2477.claim: In former colonies, instrumented democracy raises primary schooling, while instrumented political decentralization (local democracy) raises secondary and higher enrollment and average years of schooling.
2477.treatment_desc: political decentralization (local democracy: directly elected local executive and legislature), instrumented by the number of native cultures before colonization; democracy (Polity) instrumented by settler mortality and 1500 population density
2477.outcome_desc: average years of schooling of adults over 15 and secondary and higher enrollment rates, 1985-1995; primary enrollment, 1900 and 1985-1995

setting.unit_desc: more than 50 former colonies, schooling in 1900 and averages for 1985-1995

identification.variation: number of native cultures before colonization as instrument for political decentralization; settler mortality and 1500 population density as instruments for democracy, to disentangle the two institutions
identification.threat: instruments for democracy work through a broad cluster of institutions that may include decentralization, and may act via other channels; addressed with overidentification tests and added controls

mechanisms.note: colonial conditions set the distribution of political power and persistent institutions; changing educational institutions is costly because it requires changing that distribution
democracy raises primary enrollment (quantity), consistent with enfranchisement raising public education spending
local democracy and school decentralization raise advanced schooling (quality), in line with the decentralization theorem and local efficiency pressure

settled: Colonial conditions such as settler mortality, native density and factor endowments shaped institutions that persist (Acemoglu et al. 2001, 2002; Engerman and Sokoloff 1997, 2002)
Greater enfranchisement raises public education expenditure, while inequality and fractionalization lower it (Engerman et al. 1997; Galor et al. 2008)
Resources spent on education are more strongly linked to the quantity than to the quality of education
contested: Whether enfranchisement and democracy are the main institutional drivers of schooling, as traditionally emphasized, or political decentralization matters more for advanced schooling
gaps: Whether local power can foster schooling even in countries with bad historical conditions, as in Malaysia after local elections began in the late 1960s
How to separate political decentralization from democracy when instruments work through a broad cluster of institutions
2477.data_asset: cross-country dataset of 50+ former colonies combining Barro-Lee and Cohen-Soto years of schooling, enrollment rates, 1900 primary enrollment, Polity IV democracy and a decentralization index built from Beck et al. and Polity IV
2477.scope: former colonies; democracy matters for primary enrollment (quantity) and decentralization for higher levels (quality); school-management decentralization in Latin America explains about 40% of the gap with Africa (about 3 years of schooling)

2482.claim: Brazil's Bolsa Escola cut school dropout by 8 pp, but its impact was 36% larger under first-term (re-electable) mayors than under term-limited second-term mayors, who were rewarded at the polls and ran more transparent programs.
2482.treatment_desc: mayor in first term (eligible for re-election) versus second and final term (lame duck) under the constitutional two-term limit, when implementing a decentralized conditional cash transfer
2482.outcome_desc: municipality-level program performance: impact of Bolsa Escola on school dropout of beneficiaries (larger reduction is better), estimated per municipality; also mayor reelection odds and transparent implementation practices

magnitudes.outcome: program impact on dropout, first-term vs second-term mayors (36% better)
gain in dropout reduction, first-term vs second-term mayors

setting.unit_desc: randomly selected Northeast municipalities (Ceara, Pernambuco, Paraiba, Rio Grande do Norte); school records for 290,517 children, 2 years before and 3 years under the program

identification.variation: mayor's first-term versus term-limited second-term status when the program was introduced, with per-municipality program impact estimated from beneficiary versus non-beneficiary dropout before and after
identification.threat: first-term mayors may differ in ability and experience or pursue first-term clientelist gains; checked by comparing second-term mayors with first-term mayors who got re-elected and with similar political experience

mechanisms.note: re-election incentives raise effort in program implementation, and voters reward good performance with higher re-election odds
informational advantages of decentralization pay off only when electoral rules let voters hold local officials accountable

settled: Local governments have information advantages in allocating public resources, and these advantages exist (Faguet 2004; Alderman 2002)
Politicians reap electoral rewards from public programs they can claim credit for (Levitt and Snyder 1997; Manacorda, Miguel and Vigorito 2009)
Re-election incentives shape politicians choices: US governors fiscal and environmental policy (Besley and Case 1995; List and Sturm 2006), Brazilian mayors corruption (Ferraz and Finan 2009)
contested: Whether decentralized implementation delivers its expected efficiency gains, since using local information depends on how local governments are held accountable (Seabright 1996)
Whether targeting is a good indicator of decentralized program performance, as most empirical work assumes (Ravallion 2007)
gaps: Which other mechanisms of political reward and citizen control can substitute where constitutional rules do not support electoral accountability
2482.data_asset: municipal survey plus manually matched school records for 290,517 children in 261 randomly selected municipalities, combined with Bolsa Escola payment records and 2004 mayoral election outcomes
2482.scope: first-term versus second-term mayors in the Brazilian Northeast; municipal program impacts vary widely (median -6.7 pp, range -25.5 to +10.7); ability and experience effects run opposite to the incentive effect

2584.claim: Chinese provincial governors who gain connections with Politburo Standing Committee members raise pollution (10-13% of an sd) and expand coal-fired power more when rainfall is low, consistent with promotion-driven career concerns.

magnitudes.outcome: AOT, COD and SO2 on gaining connections (10-13% of an sd range)
coal-fired power, low precipitation, connected governors
coal-fired power, low precipitation (below 75th percentile), all governors

setting.unit_desc: 30 Chinese provinces (Tibet excluded), annual and monthly panel

identification.variation: changes in governors' connections to the Politburo Standing Committee from reshuffling at the center, within province; within-governor variation; precipitation shocks to hydropower
identification.threat: connected governors may be appointed to better or worse provinces; checked with pre-trends, within-governor variation (about 10% of observations) and exogenous precipitation; official pollution data may be gamed

settled: Growth matters for officials' promotion in China, and connections are important in motivating politicians (Li and Zhou 2005; Shih et al. 2012)
Politicians face a trade-off between creating jobs and protecting the environment
China relied on an unusually large amount of polluting industry relative to its development stage (Vennemo et al. 2009)
contested: Whether China's pollution reflects structural change alone or conscious political choices by leaders, which anecdotal evidence suggests
Whether environmental neglect stems from career or electoral incentives or from rents offered by private firms in exchange for tacit permission
gaps: Whether the connection-pollution link persists after 2013, when GDP stopped being the main promotion criterion and environmental protection began to count for careers
How to measure pollution credibly when official data may be gamed by politicians, since results using official data are imprecise
2584.data_asset: panel of 30 Chinese provinces, 1993-2010, combining governors' connections built from politicians' CVs with satellite aerosol optical thickness, official COD and SO2, and electricity generation by source
2584.scope: Chinese provinces 1993-2010; governors' connections matter more than party secretaries'; connected governors raise coal power more when hydropower is constrained; findings may not fully match post-2013 data

ballots lost per IED-targeted road, accounting for rainfall (more than 7,400)

settled: Elections often fail to bring peace and instead trigger renewed fighting (Collier 2009; Dunning 2011)
Candidates use violence to mobilize core voters and intimidate opponents, especially in fragile states (Collier and Vicente 2012)
Insurgents rely on popular support and are vulnerable to civilian informing, so harming civilians is costly (Berman, Shapiro and Felter 2011; Condra and Shapiro 2012)

mechanisms.note: norm of non-payment reinforced by bailouts and by expectations of no penalty; reforms aim to change the norm that electricity is a right
customers expect no penalty for bribing officials to avoid payment; bill-collector collusion with consumers is described as a source of losses

settled: Societies redistribute toward the poor through subsidized public provision of essentials such as health, education and housing

The latent demand of firms and households for continuous, reliable electricity, which is never observed because it is never offered
2547.data_asset: Bihar feeder-level administrative data on supply hours and revenue, 2018 household billing data and a Bihar survey on payment beliefs, plus cross-country T&D loss and access data for 142 countries
2547.scope: descriptive evidence from Bihar and 142 countries; losses rise then fall with access (an electricity Kuznets curve) peaking near 40% access with 25% of power lost before billing; argued to apply across developing countries

1730.claim: Third-party reporting by large firms sustains tax enforcement despite low fines and audit rates, since one of many employees can reveal collusive evasion; firm growth with development yields the S-shaped rise in the tax take.

Whether automatic withholding and return-free tax systems weaken the employee-whistleblowing mechanism when employees no longer see what employers report

1730.scope: predicts third-party enforcement is most successful for large and complex firms; supporting evidence is aggregate stylized facts, not firm-level tests

1665.claim: Longer Ramadan fasting, from the rotating Islamic calendar, lowers output growth in Muslim countries but raises Muslims' subjective well-being, via changed work values and labor supply rather than lower productivity.

contested: Whether racial threat explains whites' political behavior or is outdated (Tesler and Sears 2010)
Whether proximity to an outgroup reduces intergroup hostility (contact theory; Allport 1954) or raises it (racial threat)
Whether racial threat arises from attitude change or from selection of individuals into contexts
gaps: Whether the effect holds when the outgroup is spatially separated and defined by class, religion or sexual orientation rather than race
How much of the effect reflects race versus other dimensions of difference such as poverty
Points of leverage for studying attitudes and behavior in newly integrated populations

Sustainable economic growth is a major contributor to regime stability

690.claim: Asks when majority rule yields a transitive social preference ordering, starting from Arrow's impossibility theorem and Black's single-peakedness result; the paper's own theorem is not in the slices.
690.treatment_desc: simple majority rule as the collective-choice rule, with restrictions on individual preference orderings such as single-peakedness
690.outcome_desc: whether majority rule produces a transitive social preference ordering over a set of alternatives; a theoretical property, nothing measured

setting.unit_desc: a society of a finite number of individuals, each with a transitive preference ordering over a set of alternatives

identification.variation: conditions on individual preference orderings under which majority rule gives a social preference ordering; only the introduction is visible

settled: With more than two alternatives, no group preference ordering can in general satisfy Arrow's five reasonable conditions (Arrow)
With one-dimensional alternatives, single-peaked preferences and an odd number of individuals, majority rule gives a transitive social ordering (Black; Arrow)
gaps: When social preference orderings under majority rule can and cannot be constructed, so that Arrow's impossibility theorem does not block further work on social choice

1381.claim: Russian cities and oblasts hit hardest by the Holocaust grew less and have lower GDP per capita and wages and more Communist voting; the authors document an association and conjecture a smaller middle class as the channel.
1381.treatment_desc: severity of the Holocaust: pre-war Jewish population share interacted with German occupation, plus change in Jewish population before and after WWII (oblasts only)
1381.outcome_desc: city population and growth (to 1989 and today), oblast GDP per capita and average wages today, Communist candidates' vote share since the Soviet collapse, and middle-class size

magnitudes.outcome: city population in 1989, average occupied city (paper: would have been about 14%

setting.unit_desc: Russian cities and oblasts (administrative units between a US county and state in size)

identification.variation: pre-war Jewish population share interacted with German occupation as a proxy for Holocaust severity, compared across cities and oblasts, with a falsification exercise
identification.threat: cities with large Jewish shares may have differed systematically, and other Russian shocks (Stalinist purges, 1932-33 famine, wartime relocation of industry) may confound

settled: The Holocaust had diverse cultural, social and psychological effects, studied by historians and other scholars
contested: Whether population collapses have long-run effects: Davis and Weinstein (2002), Miguel and Roland (2007) find none for general collapses; this paper finds them for the Holocaust
Whether the association between Holocaust severity and Russian outcomes is causal rather than due to systematic differences between regions or other Soviet-era shocks
gaps: Whether a smaller middle class is the channel linking the Holocaust to present outcomes, which the paper only conjectures
How a one-off shock to social structure generates persistently divergent economic, political and social development, as the large estimated magnitudes require
1381.data_asset: pre-war Jewish population shares and German occupation status for Russian cities and oblasts, matched to census, GDP, wage and election data
1381.scope: an association, not an established causal effect; city population and middle-class effects appear before the 1990s (negative and significant in 1959, growing over time), so not simply 1990s Jewish outmigration

2024.claim: Counties with more 1860-1920 immigration (IV: aggregate flows x railway expansion) have higher income, less poverty and unemployment, more education and urbanisation today, with no long-run social costs.
2024.treatment_desc: county exposure to European immigration in the Age of Mass Migration, instrumented by predicted immigrant share from aggregate flows interacted with railway connection
2024.outcome_desc: county incomes, unemployment, poverty, education and urban share today; short-run industrialisation, agricultural productivity and patenting; social capital, civic participation and crime

setting.unit_desc: US counties; immigration 1860-1920, with outcomes from 1920-2000 and today

identification.variation: decade-by-decade fluctuations in aggregate immigrant flows interacted with the gradual expansion of the railway network, so counties newly connected during boom vs lull decades receive different immigrant shares
identification.threat: railway connection may affect long-run development directly through specialisation and industrialisation, so railway effects are allowed to vary with GDP growth and other controls

settled: The Age of Mass Migration (1850-1920) had the highest US immigration, with more arrivals from Southern, Northern and Eastern Europe than before (Hatton and Williamson 2005)
contested: Whether long-run effects of immigration match short-run effects, which could differ in magnitude and sign
Whether immigration lowers local wages: an earlier study of US cities in 1890-1903 links greater immigration to lower wage growth
gaps: Long-run consequences of immigration, since the literature has focused on short-term effects
Whether long-run effects differ by immigrants' country of origin, which the paper does not separate
2024.data_asset: county-level immigrant shares 1860-1920 and railway network expansion, linked to county economic, social, industrialisation, agricultural and patenting outcomes
2024.scope: US counties in the Age of Mass Migration; effects of immigrants in general, not by origin; identified from counties whose immigration varied with the timing of railway connection

1831.claim: Western Ukrainian communities hit by more intense 1940s Soviet deportations vote significantly less for 'pro-Russian' parties in 2004-2014 elections: indiscriminate violence reduces long-term support for the perpetrator.
1831.treatment_desc: intensity of Stalin-era Soviet deportations from western Ukraine in the 1940s (over 250,000 people deported to Siberia while suppressing a nationalist insurgency)
1831.outcome_desc: vote for 'pro-Russian' parties (pro-Russian vote margin) in Ukrainian parliamentary elections 2004-2014, by rayon

setting.unit_desc: rayons of western Ukraine, with archival 1940s deportation counts and election results 2004-2014

identification.variation: two independent designs, an IV and a fuzzy RDD, using distance from the contiguous district with more repression as the instrument for rayon-level deportation intensity
identification.threat: identifying the effect of past violence on present voting is hard (non-random violence, spatial dependence handled with Moran-eigenvector covariates); rail networks may affect elections 70 years later via wartime military activity

mechanisms.note: violence has an intergenerational impact on political preferences, transmitted through collective identity
indiscriminate violence breeds identity-based backlash against the perpetrator rather than lasting coercive compliance

settled: Violence plays a formative role in political development (Balcells 2012; Blattman 2009; Kalyvas 2006)
contested: Whether experiences of violence consolidate or undermine the political identities of affected communities (Balcells 2012; Campbell 1998; Lupu and Peisakhin)
What effect indiscriminate violence has on its intended targets, since most research has focused on short-term military consequences
gaps: How violence affects long-term political preferences and attitudes, and whether the individual-level effect also extends to communities
The long-term political calculus of communities affected by violence, flagged as a priority for future research
1831.data_asset: archival data on Soviet state deportations from western Ukraine by rayon, matched to 2004-2014 election results
1831.scope: western Ukraine only, where the perpetrator is associated with 'pro-Russian' parties; identified from rayon-level variation in deportation intensity

964.claim: In OECD countries with mobile capital, preelectoral monetary expansions occur only under flexible exchange rates with low central bank independence, while preelectoral fiscal expansions occur under fixed exchange rates.
964.treatment_desc: elections interacted with the exchange-rate regime (fixed vs flexible) and central bank independence, under capital mobility
964.outcome_desc: preelectoral expansion in monetary policy (money supply) and in fiscal policy by incumbents

setting.unit_desc: OECD countries, pooled cross-sectional time series

identification.variation: election timing interacted with exchange-rate regime and central bank independence in pooled cross-section time-series regressions, testing a formal model
identification.threat: the model assumes capital was fully mobile in every country throughout the period; robustness models relax this

settled: Under capital mobility, monetary policy is constrained when the exchange rate is fixed and fiscal policy when it is flexible (Mundell-Fleming)
contested: Whether preelectoral monetary and fiscal expansions occur unconditionally or only under particular exchange-rate regimes and central bank independence
gaps: What form fiscal institutions should take to limit preelectoral fiscal expansion in the euro area, which remains open to discussion
Refining the model's strong Mundell-Fleming assumptions, such as full capital mobility, which the authors leave to further work
964.data_asset: OECD country panel on money supply, fiscal policy, elections, exchange-rate regimes and central bank independence
964.scope: OECD countries; monetary cycles need a flexible rate and low central bank independence, fiscal cycles occur under fixed rates and are absent under flexible rates; budget-target commitment or a strong finance minister reduces fiscal cycles

1214.claim: With social preferences the expected benefit of voting does not shrink as the electorate grows, so substantial turnout is rational even in large elections; a feedback mechanism stabilises turnout at reasonable levels.
1214.treatment_desc: voters' social preferences (concern for social welfare), with the size and importance of the election
1214.outcome_desc: model prediction of the expected utility of voting and of equilibrium turnout as a function of electorate size and election importance; no empirical outcome measured

setting.unit_desc: voters in a hypothetical population in a large election

identification.variation: rational-choice model in which a voter's social benefit is proportional to the probability of being pivotal and to the number of persons affected, with feedback from turnout to the probability of being decisive

settled: Voting in large elections cannot be explained by the selfish benefits of voting, since the probability that a vote is decisive is too low (Downs 1957; Riker)
contested: Whether voting can be rational in large elections: selfish expected-utility models say not, the paper argues social preferences make substantial turnout rational
gaps: How social preferences relate to individuals' own concerns, which future research should begin to map
1214.scope: voters with both selfish and social preferences, where social preferences dominate; less important elections are predicted to have lower turnout, with turnout stabilised under a wide range of conditions

1420.claim: Contrary to the view that poverty drives support for militancy, poor Pakistanis dislike militant groups more than the middle class, most strongly the urban poor in violent districts.
1420.treatment_desc: individual poverty (low income vs middle class), interacted with urban residence and district exposure to militant violence
1420.outcome_desc: affect toward and support for four militant organisations, measured by an endorsement experiment (support for policies endorsed by the groups) plus direct questions

magnitudes.outcome: support for policies endorsed by militant groups, low-income vs middle-class Pak
three-way interaction of urban, low income and endorsement treatment on support

setting.unit_desc: adult Pakistanis in a nationally representative survey, with respondents nested in districts

identification.variation: endorsement experiment randomising whether a policy question names a militant group's endorsement; poverty, urbanity and district violence compared across respondents
identification.threat: sensitivity of militancy causes nonresponse and social desirability bias, handled by the endorsement design; small cells in interactions and district-level violence needing clustered or hierarchical models

settled: Direct survey questions about militant groups suffer item nonresponse and social desirability bias because of their sensitivity
contested: Whether poverty is a root cause of support for extremist groups: policy debates cite it, little evidence supports it, and this paper finds the poor dislike militants more
Whether exposure to terrorist attacks lowers support for militants, which the paper only suggests for the urban poor in violent districts
gaps: Whether exposure to attacks causes the lower support among the urban poor, which the paper only suggests
Effects of violence exposure separately for rural and urban respondents, since too few sampled districts saw no violence
1420.data_asset: original 6,000-person nationally representative survey of Pakistanis with an endorsement experiment on four militant organisations, matched to district-level violence (incidents, casualties)
1420.scope: Pakistan only; dislike of militants strongest among the urban poor and those in violent districts, with the middle class less negative

2006.claim: US legislators who are women, minorities or veterans contact federal agencies around 6-9 pp more per Congress for constituents sharing their identity; female legislators' relevant service probability is 40% higher.
2006.treatment_desc: legislator identity as a woman, racial/ethnic minority or veteran (descriptive representation, not a quota), relative to the constituent's shared identity
2006.outcome_desc: legislators' interventions (communications) with federal agencies on behalf of constituents sharing their identity, from FOIA records of 88,000 member-agency communications

magnitudes.outcome: probability of contacting agencies for shared-identity constituents in a given C
probability of contacting agencies for shared-identity constituents in a given C
probability of relevant service, represented by a female vs male legislator

setting.unit_desc: members of the US Congress, 108th-113th Congress, with agency intervention records by constituent group

identification.variation: differences in agency interventions across legislators by their own gender, race/ethnicity and military service, for constituents who share vs do not share that characteristic
identification.threat: the design cannot adjudicate between causal mechanisms; simulations show it recovers a veteran effect in 75% of runs if the true effect exceeds 0.55 sd

mechanisms.note: who the legislator is changes whom they serve; shared experiences are a critical mechanism for representation, without needing political consensus

settled: Experimental work has identified causal effects of legislator identity on representation, which should show up in the daily work of Congress
contested: Whether descriptive representation improves how communities are represented through constituency service, which a vast literature debates
Whether substantive representation requires political consensus between legislator and constituents; the paper finds a lack of consensus is not necessary
gaps: Which causal mechanisms underlie identity-based constituency service, which the observational design cannot adjudicate between
2006.data_asset: 88,000 records of communication between members of Congress and federal agencies obtained through FOIA requests, 108th-113th Congress
2006.scope: US Congress; the pattern holds for women, racial/ethnic minorities and veterans, with veterans giving leverage on shared experience without political cleavage

2116.claim: Fact-checks generally raise belief accuracy without fully offsetting exposure; no systematic evidence shows misperceptions are worse than before, and many responses to misinformation threaten free speech.
2116.treatment_desc: exposure to misinformation and to corrective information or fact-checking, financial incentives for accuracy, and platform or legal responses to misinformation
2116.outcome_desc: accuracy of factual beliefs and prevalence of misperceptions about political issues, including partisan gaps in reported beliefs

setting.unit_desc: survey and experimental literature on political misperceptions, mostly US

identification.variation: narrative review of survey, experimental and meta-analytic evidence on misperceptions and corrections

settled: Meta-analyses find corrective information and fact-checking generally increase belief accuracy and reduce misperceptions, though not fully offsetting exposure
False information, misperceptions and conspiracy theories are general features of human society (Hofstadter 1964; Bowman and Rugg 2013)
contested: Whether partisan gaps in reported factual beliefs are genuine or expressive: accuracy incentives narrowed the partisan divide in some experiments (Allcott et al. 2020)
Whether a 'post-truth' era of unprecedented misperceptions exists, as moral-panic claims about 'fake news' suggest
Whether correcting facts changes attitudes: information on the true number of immigrants had little effect on immigration attitudes (Hopkins et al. 2019)
gaps: Systematic evidence on whether the prevalence of misperceptions today is worse than in the past, which does not exist
2116.scope: mostly US evidence; corrections work on average but do not fully offset exposure to misinformation; exposure to untrustworthy websites was limited for most Americans in 2016

931.claim: In a vote-buying model, presidential veto power and bicameral separation push a chamber to create internal veto players or supermajority rules, while a unicameral structure encourages delegating power to a leader.
931.treatment_desc: constitutional structure: unicameral vs bicameral legislature and presidential veto power, as extra chambers able to block bills
931.outcome_desc: model prediction of the internal organisation of a legislative chamber: hurdle factors via internal veto players or supermajority rules vs delegation of decision rights to a leader; nothing measured

setting.unit_desc: legislative chambers and a veto-wielding president in a game of delegating decision rights

identification.variation: vote-buying model of delegation of decision rights in a game among chambers, with the power to block a bill captured by hurdle factors; numerical lognormal examples

mechanisms.note: a vote-buying model shows how veto power and bicameral separation change a chamber's incentive to raise internal hurdles or centralise decision power

settled: Legislative voting rules in constitutions are with few exceptions anonymous and egalitarian, yet actual legislatures have varied internal organisational structures
Existing theories of legislative organisation mainly explain why committee systems emerge in the US Congress
gaps: Why legislative organisation varies across countries' legislatures, which theories focused on the US Congress do not explain
Why one legislative structure is chosen over another with the same hurdle factors, which is beyond the scope of the model
Whether the same approach explains the internal organisation of legislative parties and factions
931.scope: simple model ranking legislative structures by the incentive to centralise power; supermajority rules in one chamber may lead to internal veto players in the other chamber

1691.claim: Support for redistribution has two facets: taking from the rich tracks income self-interest, while giving to the poor tracks other-oriented social affinity, which reconciles conflicting self-interest and solidarity findings.
1691.treatment_desc: individual income (self-interest) and social affinity with welfare beneficiaries as predictors of two separate dimensions of redistribution attitudes
1691.outcome_desc: attitudes toward redistribution conceived as taking from the rich ('redistribution from') vs giving to the poor ('redistribution to'), from survey items and factor analysis

setting.unit_desc: British survey respondents in a longitudinal attitude series asked since 1986, plus respondents in four European countries in 2008

identification.variation: exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis of survey items separating the 'redistribution from' and 'redistribution to' dimensions, then comparing how income stratifies each
identification.threat: the item explicitly mentioning redistribution loads on both factors from the early 2000s but not earlier

mechanisms.note: self-interest explains support for taking from the rich but not giving to the poor, which follows social affinity

settled: Most political economy models treat economic self-interest as a key predictor of support for income redistribution
Modern welfare states face financial pressure from rising inequality, declining revenues and growing expenses
contested: Whether support for redistribution is driven by economic self-interest or by other-oriented concerns such as solidarity and affinity for the poor, which yield conflicting predictions
Whether demand for redistribution is unidimensional; the paper argues the tension is partly an artefact of treating it so
gaps: Determinants of social affinity and altruism, needed to understand attitudes toward redistribution to the poor
How the two facets explain changes in mass support for welfare policy and the mixed pattern of resilience and retrenchment
1691.data_asset: British longitudinal attitude survey items asked since 1986, plus cross-sectional survey data from four European countries in 2008
1691.scope: UK and four advanced European countries; income stratifies attitudes toward redistribution from the rich but not toward giving to the poor

1434.claim: Competition among senders does not generally increase information revealed; Blackwell-connectedness of the information environment is necessary and sufficient for equilibria to be no less informative than collusion.
1434.treatment_desc: competition among information senders: the number of senders and the alignment of their preferences, given the set of signals available to each
1434.outcome_desc: model prediction of how informative equilibrium outcomes are relative to the collusive outcome, and whether adding senders or reducing preference alignment raises information revealed

setting.unit_desc: several senders choosing which signals to communicate to a receiver in a symmetric-information game

identification.variation: symmetric-information games where senders commit to truthfully communicating chosen signals; equilibrium compared with the collusive outcome under the Blackwell order

mechanisms.note: competition raises information only when the information environment is Blackwell-connected, not as a general result of strategic communication
competition in the marketplace of ideas need not increase information revealed, which qualifies the case for media ownership regulation and press freedom

settled: Competition can raise information revelation in verifiable-message games (Milgrom and Roberts 1986; Shin 1998) and in multidimensional cheap talk with two senders (Battaglini 2002)
contested: Whether competition among senders increases the information revealed, as a long tradition in political and legal thought holds, which the paper finds ambiguous in general
Whether adding senders or reducing the alignment of their preferences necessarily increases information revealed, which holds only under Blackwell-connectedness
gaps: Full characterisations and comparative statics for cheap-talk and disclosure settings with multiple senders, which their strategic complexity leaves incomplete (Sobel 2013)
Whether the competition results hold when senders cannot commit to truthful communication, which the model sets aside
1434.scope: senders can commit to truthful communication and incentive compatibility is set aside; results hold for any preferences once the information environment is Blackwell-connected

1096.claim: Contribution limits and matching public funds can be Pareto improving even with truthful ads and rational voters: unrestricted contributions make voters rationally cynical, undermining the effectiveness of campaign spending.
1096.treatment_desc: contribution limits and matching public financing of campaigns, against unrestricted interest-group contributions
1096.outcome_desc: model prediction of citizens' welfare (Pareto improvement), the effectiveness of campaign advertising, and the level of policy favours promised to contributors

identification.variation: equilibrium model of campaign advertising with interest-group contributions, policy favours and rational voters, comparing unrestricted contributions with limits plus matching public funds

mechanisms.note: contributions buy policy favours, which makes voters cynical; the model departs from common-agency lobbying models (Bernheim and Whinston 1986; Grossman and Helpman 1994) on a key assumption
advertising can help elect more qualified leaders, but unrestricted contributions weaken this selection benefit by lowering vote-switching

settled: Interest groups supply campaign contributions and candidates can offer policy favours to attract higher contributions (assumed)
contested: Whether campaign finance limits can be justified when advertising conveys truthful information and voters are rational, which the paper argues they can
1096.scope: candidates with a strong desire to hold office; as that desire becomes infinitely strong, campaign spending is completely ineffective and limits can leave all citizens better off

1830.claim: Russian TV availability in Ukraine raised pro-Russian vote share by about 7.5 pp in 2014 via persuasion, not mobilisation; effects were largest among pro-Russian-prior voters and counter-effective among strongly pro-Western ones.
1830.treatment_desc: exposure to Russian state television, a conspicuously biased source, proxied by availability of the Russian analog TV signal
1830.outcome_desc: precinct-level vote share for 'pro-Russian' parties and candidates in the 2014 presidential and parliamentary elections; survey political attitudes

support for pro-Russian parties, presidential election, per 1 sd of Russian TV r
support for pro-Russian parties, parliamentary election, per 1 sd of Russian TV

setting.unit_desc: Ukrainian polling precincts in the 2014 elections, plus individual respondents in an original survey

Whether biased media effects come from persuasion or differential mobilisation, which the paper's evidence suggests is persuasion

The true nature of heterogeneity in biased-media effects, a methodologically challenging issue for future research

1830.scope: Ukraine in the 2014 elections, a highly polarised society; the average effect works through voters with pro-Russian priors, with biased media polarising a society that is already polarised

2108.claim: Citizens of 18 consolidated European democracies continue to endorse self-governance, with stable democratic preferences and growing institutional confidence, though 'democrats in name only' grow among the young in some countries.
2108.treatment_desc: birth cohort, age and survey period (age-period-cohort variation in democratic support over time)
2108.outcome_desc: citizens' democratic regime preferences, importance of living in a democracy, confidence in democratic institutions and authoritarian regime preferences

setting.unit_desc: survey respondents in 18 consolidated European democracies (countries not named in the slices)

identification.variation: age-period-cohort analysis of repeated cross-national survey data, separating age, cohort and period effects
identification.threat: risk of cherry-picked findings, addressed by pre-registered analyses and transparent reporting of all evidence

contested: Whether Western citizens are turning their backs on democracy, as recent studies argue, or still support it, as these survey data show
Whether younger cohorts are less opposed to regimes at odds with liberal democracy, which holds in some but not all countries

What citizens mean by democracy across its multi-faceted components, now that support for the generic concept is not the main question
2108.data_asset: new cross-national survey data from 18 European countries, 1981-2018, on democratic regime preferences, institutional trust and political interest, analysed under a pre-analysis plan
2108.scope: 18 consolidated European democracies; stable aggregate support, with 'democrats in name only' rising among the youngest cohorts in some but not all countries

934.claim: Among industrial democracies since 1974, politicians in systems where elections decisively determine government and defeat is costly avoid fixed exchange rates; coalition systems use fixes as a focal point.
934.treatment_desc: domestic political institutions: how decisively the electoral system determines government (majoritarian vs proportional, coalition systems) and the cost of electoral defeat

mechanisms.note: credible-commitment and policy-capability arguments predict majoritarian systems fix more than PR systems; the results show the opposite

Whether governments must kowtow to international capital or internationalisation instead alters domestic groups' policy demands
gaps: Domestic political sources of exchange-rate regime choice, which the international political economy literature has treated mainly through the presence of an international hegemon
934.data_asset: country-year data on exchange-rate arrangements of industrial democracies since 1974 with measures of domestic political institutions
934.scope: industrial democracies since 1974; domestic institutions explain floating vs fixing but not the choice between a unilateral fix and joining a multilateral agreement, where Europe/EC membership and the prior arrangement matter

identification.variation: cross-individual and cross-country variation in consumption patterns, skills and sector, in multilevel random-coefficient models of trade-policy attitudes

settled: Under Heckscher-Ohlin trade theory liberalisation raises real wages of the abundant factor and lowers those of the scarce factor, which has dominated the literature on trade attitudes
contested: Whether trade policy beliefs reflect only labour-market position or also consumer tastes, which political economists have tended to ignore

Whether rural-urban support for free trade differs by land vs capital abundance, a tentative finding
1117.data_asset: survey data from 41 nations on trade policy attitudes, consumption patterns and labour-market position

1376.claim: Incentives crowd out rare, heroic behaviours but crowd in common ones, so optimal incentives depart from Pigou-Ramsey taxation; norms-based interventions face credibility limits and laws express societal values.
1376.treatment_desc: social norms (honour, stigma, social sanctions and rewards) interacting with material incentives and laws, including norms-based campaigns and the expressive role of law

identification.variation: signalling model with a social multiplier (reputational payoffs depend on behaviour frequency) and an informational multiplier (perceptions of norms shaped by an informed principal's policies)

mechanisms.note: norms arise from individuals' behaviours and inferences and interact with incentives and law, so incentives can shift norms through crowding in or out
an informed principal's messages and policies convey information about societal preferences, but credibility limits norms-based interventions when descriptive and prescriptive norms conflict

settled: Material incentives often work but can fail through crowding out or have disproportionate effects through crowding in
Social psychology offers a wide base of experimental regularities on norms-based interventions but no clear analytical framework
contested: Whether law merely prices behaviour or also expresses and shapes societal values, a spectrum from pure consequentialists to pure expressivists
Whether incentives crowd out or crowd in intrinsic motivation, which the model ties to how rare or common the behaviour is
gaps: The coevolution of norms, law and the social meaning of private and public actions, a vast and promising topic for future research
1376.scope: incentives crowd out rare heroic behaviours and crowd in common respectable ones; expressive concerns weaken incentives when the principal's information is about society's goodness and strengthen them when about spillovers

1940.claim: Excluding almost half a million Mexican bracero farm workers did not raise US farm wages or employment: zero labor market impact cannot be rejected, inconsistent with a model with no change in technology or crop mix.

settled: The effects of active labor market policy on workers' wages and employment have been widely evaluated (LaLonde 2016)
contested: Whether labor scarcity raises wages or has ambiguous or even perverse effects under endogenous technical advance, as recent theory suggests
Whether immigration barriers raise domestic wages and employment, as the bracero exclusion was intended to
gaps: Other natural experiments to test causal links between labor scarcity and endogenous technical change, as urged by Acemoglu (2010)
1940.data_asset: novel labor market data measuring state-level exposure to the bracero exclusion and farm wages and employment

contested: Whether the pivotal voter model describes turnout, the most extensively studied and debated theory in political science (Green and Shapiro 1994)
Whether election closeness is a valid test of the model, since simple tests are not nuanced enough (Battaglini, Morton and Palfrey 2005)
gaps: Field tests of the pivotal voter model, since voting costs, benefits and beliefs about being pivotal are unobservable in field data

target candidate vote choice (not statistically significant)

Racial heterogeneity decreases social capital (Alesina and La Ferrara 2000)

People support redistribution less when it aids other races, and ethnically divided places redistribute less (Luttmer 2001; Alesina and Glaeser 2004)

1466.claim: In a model of elections as public signals in a revolution game, citizens discount fraud, so monitoring lowers equilibrium fraud without raising the chance of deposing incumbents; elections may be held only because of monitoring.

gaps: Why relatively insecure incumbents, who tend to do worse in elections, still hold them, a hard question in this formulation

Whether elections are valuable to a wider range of leaders if incumbents can also use election information, for concessions or consolidating power

Whether headline haircuts measure debt relief, since the sovereign's debt value fell 60% after Greece's 65% haircut but rose 5% after Uruguay's 13% haircut

Why governments discriminate between creditors in some defaults but not others, and whether domestic creditors get better treatment on average
How domestic political cleavages, measurable with public opinion polls, affect the incentive to default
How to reconcile contradictory findings on the effect of electoral democracy on debt
How to close the gap between theories of sovereign debt and the data used to test them

1173.claim: An incumbency advantage in fundraising can deter challengers; matching public funds improve voter welfare in districts with advertising but can reduce it elsewhere, so optimal campaign finance policy depends on the incumbent's lead.

settled: Candidates solicit interest-group contributions secured by promised favours, a maintained assumption of the model
Campaign finance reforms have both positive and negative welfare effects on moderate voters in the prior literature
contested: Whether public financing or a ban on contributions improves voter welfare, as many reformers think; here it depends on the degree of incumbency advantage

1825.claim: Matching income registry records to an election survey, voters who appear sociotropic vote equally on personal finances; partisan bias and economic information both shape evaluations, and results are inconsistent with myopic voting.

Whether voters are myopic, as survey-based work concludes, or project the future well, as macro-based work argues

Whether national economic evaluations reflect information about one's own circumstances from other sources, which would explain apparent sociotropic voting

1825.scope: Sweden around the 2006 election; sign of the pocketbook effect is not stated in the slices; apparent sociotropic voters also vote on personal finances

How the diffuse preferences of labor interests are aggregated into policy outcomes in the politics of protection
How occupation shapes both the distributional consequences of trade and preferences toward trade openness

1582.claim: Gifts are structured by three co-existing moral principles of economic relations, communism, exchange and hierarchy, which ordinary people combine in every society, while dominant economic forms elevate one above the others.

1621.claim: Old Bailey trials for violent and nonviolent offences, semantically indistinguishable in the late 18th century, grew steadily more distinct, driven by gradual cultural change rather than any specific legislative or bureaucratic change.

1794.claim: Survey: referendum approval of new spending or debt uniformly lowers both; the initiative lowers spending and taxes in US states and Swiss cantons but raises spending in cities, and brings policy closer to majority opinion.

mechanisms.note: policies are more congruent with majority opinion in initiative states, suggesting the majority counteracts special interests

The initiative is consistently associated with more conservative social policies
Policy is more congruent with majority opinion in initiative states than in states without the initiative
contested: Whether the initiative raises or lowers spending: lower in US states and Swiss cantons but higher in cities

1937.claim: Emigration to the US, instrumented by frost shocks and travel costs, raised labor-movement membership, strikes, turnout and left voting in Swedish municipalities, plus welfare spending and adoption of representative democracy.

identification.variation: severe local frost shocks that sparked an initial emigration wave, interacted with within-country travel costs, predict emigration over decades

contested: Whether emigration inhibits the use of political voice or instead raises demand for political change

1554.claim: Model: misperceived good actions start conflict spirals that contain the seeds of their own dissolution, since Bayesian agents eventually infer the spiral began by mistake and experiment with a good action, restarting the cycle.
1554.treatment_desc: misperception of good actions as bad, with limited information about past actions, in sequential coordination games between two groups
1554.outcome_desc: model prediction for the onset, duration and recurrence of inter-group conflict spirals; no empirical estimate

setting.unit_desc: overlapping generations of agents from two groups

identification.variation: overlapping-generations model in which agents of two groups play coordination games under incomplete information about whether the other side is a bad type who always takes bad actions

mechanisms.note: conflict arises from fear and distrust: each side expects bad actions and misreads good ones, as in the Hobbesian spiral view

settled: Inter-group conflict is pervasive despite mutual benefits from trust and cooperation
Conflict can stem from fear and distrust, with each side seeing war as inevitable and unwilling to cede the first-mover advantage (Thucydides)

998.claim: In 900+ FCC lobbying contacts on 101 issues, large firms' amount and organisation of lobbying fit transaction-cost and collective-action predictions; small firms' do not, though they lobby less when proprietary information is at risk.

998.data_asset: new dataset of over 900 lobbying contacts covering 101 issues at the Federal Communications Commission in early 1998
998.scope: large firms behave as theory predicts and small firms do not; one agency (FCC) in early 1998; small firms lobby less when they must reveal proprietary information

1853.claim: Overview of EU-28 labor-market reforms since the 2008/09 crisis (dismissal protection, unemployment benefits, ALMPs) asking whether they made labor markets less dualized; the slices give no verdict.

managerial employment vs control mean (stated as more than 19%)

2249.claim: Model: democracy is sustainable when opposing politicians are neither very attractive nor very unattractive; backsliding occurs when citizens knowingly consent to a highly appealing incumbent or unconditionally oppose him.

2092.claim: Model: an autocrat holds fair elections to signal his popularity; more elite repression of the opposition makes fair elections less likely, while a higher cost of protesting for ordinary citizens makes them more likely.
2092.treatment_desc: elite repression of opposition leaders and the cost to ordinary citizens of protesting (cruelty toward common people)

1632.claim: General framework for institutional dynamics under stochastic shifts in payoffs and political power: with ordered states and single-crossing conditions a Markov voting equilibrium exists; applied to repression and experimentation.

1984.claim: In four pre-registered dictator-game experiments (N = 3591), thinking about karma or God reduced selfishness among believers, not non-believers, moving initially selfish offers toward fairness and leaving fair offers unchanged.
