1416.scope: post-Bretton Woods country-years; the negative democracy-fixity link strengthens with domestic-oriented median voters and with societal groups' ability to influence policy

1996.claim: Mass purges are top-down accountability in autocracy: more violence always raises subordinates' performance but improves selection only if violence starts low; the share purged is non-monotonic in violence.
1996.treatment_desc: mass purge of party members and bureaucrats by an autocrat, with the intensity of violence against the purged as the policy parameter
1996.outcome_desc: agents' performance (effort), selection of subordinates, and the proportion of agents purged, as functions of the intensity of violence

setting.unit_desc: model of an autocrat and many agents; illustrated with the Soviet purges, the Cultural Revolution and the Erdogan purge

identification.variation: principal-agent model with moral hazard and adverse selection in which the autocrat motivates and screens agents by purging them

mechanisms.note: violence always raises agents' performance but improves selection only when violence is low to begin with; purge breadth is non-monotonic in violence
even absent de jure checks, the autocrat is de facto constrained by her subordinates' strategic behaviour

settled: Coercion can serve as an incentive device in a principal-agent relationship, e.g. a slave-owner cutting a slave's outside option (Acemoglu and Wolitzky 2011)
Autocracies have used mass purges of party members and bureaucrats, including the Soviet purges, the Cultural Revolution and the Erdogan purge
contested: Whether mass purges serve as top-down accountability, motivating and screening many agents, as the paper contends
gaps: How elite purges and mass purges connect, possibly building on this framework
1996.scope: in mild purges the purged set is delineated by performance, in violent purges no performance indicator guarantees safety; results also hold for discriminate purges

1571.claim: After the largest military victories against the FARC, Colombia's government cut counterinsurgency activity, especially in electorally salient municipalities: politicians need enemies alive to keep their advantage.
1571.treatment_desc: major events in the Colombian civil war that raised the probability of defeating the guerrillas, interacted with municipalities where voters were most electorally responsive
1571.outcome_desc: government military activity against the guerrillas (counterinsurgency effort) in the municipality after the events

setting.unit_desc: Colombian municipalities observed before and after major events against the FARC

identification.variation: timing of major events against the FARC (post-event dummies) interacted with municipal electoral salience, with municipality fixed effects
identification.threat: differential trends in municipalities correlated with electoral responsiveness, reaction to guerrilla activity, build-up time for operations, army incentives; each is checked

mechanisms.note: re-election incentives can discourage finishing a task: an incumbent with a comparative advantage underperforms to keep his electoral advantage
cuts in military activity concentrate in electorally salient places where voters are most responsive

settled: Unlike paramilitaries, the FARC do not systematically influence electoral outcomes (Acemoglu et al. 2013)
An agent hired to finish a task puts himself out of a job by finishing it, and a politician elected as the person for the job may be replaced once it is done
contested: Whether the post-victory drop in military activity reflects electoral incentives rather than guerrilla activity, build-up time or army incentives; the paper favours electoral incentives
1571.data_asset: municipality-level data on government military activity against the guerrillas; Noche y Niebla (press and NGO reports) is one primary source
1571.scope: the drop follows major events and is concentrated in electorally salient municipalities; stable across estimation windows of 6 to 24 months; only events that make a guerrilla defeat more likely matter

2048.claim: Disadvantaged-group bureaucrats recruited via affirmative action in the Indian Administrative Service perform no worse than others on district MGNREGA implementation; a 1-sd rise in their share moves it by 0.013 SD.
2048.treatment_desc: proportion of affirmative-action (caste-reserved) recruits among the IAS officers serving in a district
2048.outcome_desc: log number of households receiving at least 100 days of employment under MGNREGA in the district, as bureaucratic performance

magnitudes.outcome: log households with 100+ days of MGNREGA work, per 1-sd rise in affirmative-acti

setting.unit_desc: Indian districts, with IAS officers' recruitment records, backgrounds and careers matched to MGNREGA implementation

identification.variation: instrument for the proportion of affirmative-action officers in a district (first-stage correlation 0.6), with a discontinuity comparison near the exam cutoff as an alternative
identification.threat: affirmative-action and general officers differ in exam quality and may be assigned to districts non-randomly; balance tests and a cutoff comparison are used

mechanisms.note: the null may mask opposing effects: disadvantaged officers recruited on merit raise provision, neutralized for affirmative-action recruits with exam ranks 83 and higher

settled: Affirmative action has been widely studied in education and politics (Arcidiacono 2005; Bertrand, Hanna and Mullainathan 2010; Besley et al. 2004; Bhavnani 2009)
contested: Whether affirmative action worsens bureaucratic performance by lowering recruit quality (Griffin 1992; Lewis 1997; Lott 2000) or improves it through more representative, responsive recruits
gaps: Effects of affirmative-action quotas in bureaucratic promotions, which might differ from effects at recruitment
Effects of affirmative-action quotas on the honesty of bureaucrats
Whether the null extends beyond one programme (MGNREGA) and one elite service (the IAS)
2048.data_asset: detailed data on recruitment, background and careers of Indian Administrative Service officers, matched to district-level MGNREGA implementation
2048.scope: one programme (MGNREGA) in one elite service; the null may mask opposing effects, with merit-recruited disadvantaged officers associated with somewhat higher provision

2091.claim: Democracy survives when the opposition can rally citizens to deter incumbent abuse without crying wolf; non-winner-take-all institutions, accurate media, low partisanship and democratic values usually help, but not always.
2091.treatment_desc: conditions of a model of incumbent abuse: non-winner-take-all institutions, media accuracy, citizens' partisanship and support for democracy
2091.outcome_desc: democratic survival: incumbent abuse or breakdown, opposition calls for protest, and citizen protest that deters elites

setting.unit_desc: formal model of an incumbent, an opposition and citizens; motivated by 43 democratic breakdowns in 1975-2016 and erosion in Hungary, Poland, Nicaragua and Turkey

identification.variation: formal model in which the opposition can call for protest, citizens choose whether to protest, and extensions allow erosion, fake news and strategic inflaming of partisanship

mechanisms.note: deterrence needs an opposition that calls protest only when abuse occurs; cry-wolf incentives and partisanship can break citizens' coordinated punishment
accurate media on leaders' behaviour promotes survival; with low accuracy higher democratic values can threaten democracy

settled: Incumbent abuse is the most common modern initiator of democratic breakdown; 43 democracies broke down from 1975 to 2016
contested: Whether citizens punish antidemocratic acts: a Hungarian survey experiment found information on Fidesz's antidemocratic reforms had little effect on approval (Ahlquist et al. 2018)
How strongly Americans value democratic norms over partisanship, which is under ongoing debate
gaps: Whether winner-take-all US institutions face increasing strain or continue to coexist with constrained executive power
2091.scope: with low information quality, higher democracy support and lower partisanship can threaten democracy; higher elite valuation of future payoffs typically undermines it

1980.claim: Rural elites' 1960s transfers of land into waqf to avoid expropriation entrenched Islamism in Indonesia: greater expropriation threat raised Islamist party votes, the religious sector and local sharia laws, not piety.
1980.treatment_desc: threat of land expropriation under the early-1960s land reform, which led landowners to transfer land into waqf (inalienable religious endowments)
1980.outcome_desc: electoral support for Islamist parties (vote share) in regions facing different expropriation threats; also size of the religious sector and local sharia laws

setting.unit_desc: Indonesian regions, with 1960 population density as the running variable for expropriation intensity

identification.variation: regional exposure to the 1960 land reform's expropriation threat, set by population-density cutoffs (50, 250 and 400 people/km2), not a simple RD since waqf shows no jump at the cutoff
identification.threat: density cutoffs could be manipulated or reflect pre-reform Islamic strength; McCrary test and pre-reform balance checks reported; mismeasured marginal holdings bias toward zero

mechanisms.note: waqf endowments gave conservative forces the capital and organisation to promote Islamist ideology and mobilise against the secular state
institutional shocks in the religious sphere led to downstream cultural and political change, reversing the usual culture-to-institutions direction (Greif 1994)

settled: Religion has been a driving force of historical change, and religious influence in public life has grown worldwide, with a rise in support for Islamism in the Muslim world
Dissolving religiously owned monastery lands in 15th-century England raised innovation and growth (Heldring, Robinson and Vollmer 2017)
contested: Whether culture drives institutional change (Greif 1994) or religious-sphere institutions drive cultural and political change, as found here
Whether Islamist support reflects greater piety or greater demand for religion in government; the paper finds the latter
gaps: Whether religious competition moderates Islamism in Muslim countries like Indonesia, and what role the waqf plays in this process
How specific religious institutions shape political activism by religious actors, which the economics of religion has rarely studied
1980.data_asset: contemporary waqf land and endowed Islamic institutions, census tabulations of 1960s landholdings, Islamist party vote shares and local sharia laws
1980.scope: identified from regional exposure to the 1960 land reform threat; works through demand for religion in government, not piety; waqf assets also lower agricultural productivity

1432.claim: In a model where candidates belong to intraparty factions that compete to direct local public goods, spending favours party strongholds and inefficient policies persist; Mexican water-connection data support several predictions.
1432.treatment_desc: intraparty factions (hierarchical networks of party officials) competing before elections to direct local public goods to their constituencies
1432.outcome_desc: allocation of local public goods across places: water inlet and sewage connections per capita in municipalities, bias toward party strongholds, persistence

setting.unit_desc: balanced panel of potable water inlet and sewage outlet connections in 463 municipalities

identification.variation: model of intraparty factional competition, with predictions checked on connection counts around governors' elections and on governors' later promotion

mechanisms.note: officials use public resources to advance their careers within the party; later party success relates to the vote share won
actual, not formal, power to procure public goods sits with party factions rather than elected office, distorting allocation beyond formal rules

settled: Public spending tends to favour incumbent party strongholds, a bias reported in many cross-sectional empirical studies
contested: Whether standard models of electoral resource allocation, which treat candidates or parties as unitary singletons, fit the data: tests have produced mixed results
gaps: How intra-party career incentives shape the allocation of public resources, a 'political personnel economics' of parties
Better data on politicians' later party careers to test whether delivering resources buys advancement (only limited data used)
1432.data_asset: newly coded panel of potable water inlet and sewage outlet connections in 463 Mexican municipalities, 1994-2001
1432.scope: factions accentuate but are not the only source of the stronghold premium; the empirical test covers one service (water) in Mexican municipalities

1767.claim: Since the 1990s Sweden, Germany and Korea retrenched unemployment protection and deregulated temporary work as employers withdrew from cross-class settlements, challenging the varieties-of-capitalism 'limited movement' view.
1767.treatment_desc: early-1990s economic crisis, globalization pressure and persistent unemployment, which shifted bargaining power toward employers in coordinated market economies
1767.outcome_desc: labor market reform: retrenchment of unemployment protection, workfare, and deregulation of temporary and regular employment

setting.unit_desc: three coordinated market economies compared: Sweden, Germany and South Korea

identification.variation: comparative case study of labor market and welfare reform in three coordinated market economies since the 1990s, tracing employer and union positions

settled: Coordinated market economies rested on a post-war cross-class compromise that sustained generous social policy and the full-employment objective
Unions and skilled workers often preferred Bismarckian earnings-related protection to Swedish-style egalitarianism, as a better deal for industrial workers
contested: Whether coordinated market economies show only 'limited movement' under globalization (varieties of capitalism); the paper finds far-reaching change since the 1990s
Whether partisan differences still shape welfare reform: the decline in partisan difference put trade unions further on the defensive
1767.data_asset: comparative case material on labor market and welfare reform in Sweden, Germany and South Korea, including employer federation and parliamentary documents
1767.scope: three coordinated market economies; labor market insiders in Germany and Sweden were spared deregulation, while regular workers in Korea also lost employment protection

2303.claim: A dynamic model with granular geography shows topography alone is sufficient, but not necessary, to generate European polycentrism and Chinese unification; a high-productivity northern Chinese core delivers the same result.
2303.treatment_desc: fractured land: topographical barriers and the location of productive agricultural land (geography) in a dynamic model of state formation in Eurasia
2303.outcome_desc: number, size and political consolidation of polities over simulated time, compared with historical outcomes in Europe, China, Africa and the Americas

setting.unit_desc: simulated map of Eurasia over 500 periods ending in 1500, with Africa and the Americas as comparison

identification.variation: dynamic state-formation model on a map with granular topography and productive land, simulated and compared with history, with counterfactual maps (no obstacles, uniform resources)
identification.threat: the simplest fractured-land model misses the slow state formation seen in Africa and the Americas; sensitivity tests use alternative resource measures

settled: Western Europe's economic rise is often attributed to its polycentric state system (Jones 2003; Mokyr 2016; Scheidel 2019)
Geography can shape economic outcomes directly through access to trade routes or exposure to disease vectors
contested: Whether fractured land (topography) or land productivity, such as a high-productivity northern Chinese core, explains European polycentrism and Chinese unification (Diamond 1997)
Whether the fractured-land logic explains slow state formation in Africa and the Americas, which the simplest version misses
gaps: How military technological change, investment in state capacity and epidemic disease affect state formation in a fractured-land model
Probability distributions of historical outcomes generated by the model, left beyond the scope of the paper
Why state formation was slow in Africa and the Americas relative to the simplest model
2303.data_asset: granular geographic data on topography and the location of productive agricultural land in Eurasia, with agricultural productivity and historical population as robustness measures
2303.scope: Eurasia, calibrated baseline and preferred specification; topography alone suffices but is not necessary; theory and data diverge in Africa and the Americas

1198.claim: In the Danish (2000) and Swedish (2003) euro referendums, economic calculation shaped votes most clearly in Sweden, where a fixed-versus-floating regime was at stake, while political community mattered strongly in both.
1198.treatment_desc: individual-level economic calculation (stakes in the exchange rate regime) and political community (identity with Europe and the EU)
1198.outcome_desc: individual vote on euro adoption in the Danish and Swedish referendums, with euro preferences separated from EU preferences

setting.unit_desc: voters in exit polls of the Danish (2000) and Swedish (2003) euro referendums

identification.variation: individual exit-poll responses in two referendums with different exchange-rate stakes (Denmark fixed to fixed, Sweden floating to fixed), estimated by multinomial logit
identification.threat: preferences over the euro are entangled with preferences over the EU, so the multinomial logit separates them

settled: The political economy of exchange rate arrangements has grown rapidly over the past decade
The trade-off between expertise and control has been widely debated in the central bank independence literature
contested: Whether euro preferences are driven by economic calculation or by political community: calculation operates where the regime choice is at stake, community in both cases
Whether existing work on euro attitudes separates preferences for the euro from preferences for the EU, which this paper criticises
gaps: The democratic contours and implications of exchange rate regimes and currency choices themselves, which are much less understood than central bank independence
Separating attitudes toward the EU and the euro and identifying their behavioural determinants, as in a future Polish referendum
1198.data_asset: exit polling data from the Danish (2000) and Swedish (2003) euro referendums, the Swedish data from the Valu exit polls
1198.scope: two cases: Denmark (fixed to fixed) and Sweden (floating to fixed); calculation operates most clearly in Sweden, community in both

1939.claim: Gulf states admitting many low-wage migrants cut global inequality far more per capita than OECD welfare states; OECD imitation would beat full internal equalisation, a trade-off between openness and equality.
1939.treatment_desc: openness to low-wage migration: mass admission of migrants (GCC countries) vs 'fortress welfare state' policy (OECD countries)
1939.outcome_desc: global (between-country) income inequality, measured by the mean log deviation, vs inequality within receiving countries

setting.unit_desc: GCC and OECD receiving countries, including developed countries above mean world income (Figure 3)

identification.variation: descriptive comparison of per-capita reductions in global inequality through migration and remittances in GCC vs OECD countries, plus calibrated counterfactuals of OECD countries imitating the GCC
identification.threat: estimates are highly imprecise and mix guesswork with facts; the deterrent effect of taxes on earnings is ignored and labour-supply elasticities in developing countries are unmeasured

settled: Inequality across nations is possibly much greater than inequality within nations (Bourguignon and Morrisson 2002; Sala-i-Martin 2006; Milanovic 2015)
Most of the potential value of redistributive social insurance lies in transfers across rather than within nations (Kopczuk et al. 2005)
contested: Whether global and domestic egalitarianism imply the same policy: the paper argues global egalitarianism contradicts naive domestic egalitarianism, even in empirically plausible cases
Whether deontological moral constraints in liberal theory should rule out GCC-style migration arrangements, which the proposal would violate
gaps: The extent and nature of transfers within and between nations and their effect on inequality, poorly measured especially for developing and authoritarian countries
Labour supply elasticities in developing countries and efficiency losses from capture, corruption and waste in transfers, which are largely unmeasured
How feasible and practical a migration-based approach to global redistribution is, left for future research
1939.data_asset: newly available data on migration and remittances (Naidu et al. 2016) for GCC and OECD countries
1939.scope: illustrative: all estimated quantities are highly imprecise and mix guesswork with facts; assumes migration at this scale lowers wages to $9,000

2099.claim: In a model where parties choose turnout norms enforced by costly peer punishment, the larger party wins when enforcement is cheap; with costly enforcement and few committed voters the smaller party may win, as Olson predicts.
2099.treatment_desc: cost of monitoring and peer punishment needed to enforce a collectively chosen turnout norm, and party size, in a two-party election
2099.outcome_desc: turnout of each party's voters and the electoral advantage of the larger vs the smaller party

setting.unit_desc: model of a two-party election where each party's voters adopt a participation norm

identification.variation: game-theoretic model in which competing parties choose turnout norms that members enforce through costly peer monitoring and punishment

mechanisms.note: the small group's advantage (Olson) arises only with high monitoring costs and few committed voters; with low costs the larger party is advantaged

settled: Social norms and peer pressure play a key role in voter participation (Della Vigna et al. 2014; Gerber, Green and Larimer 2008; Amat et al. 2018)
In the ethical voter model, individuals adopt the participation-rate norm their party would most prefer (Feddersen and Sandroni 2006; Coate and Conlin 2004)
contested: Whether the larger or smaller party has the turnout advantage: ethical-voting theories favour the large group, but with costly enforcement the small group can win
gaps: Whether the peer-punishment model of group turnout explains street demonstrations, strikes and lobbying by bribery, to which it potentially applies
2099.scope: two-party elections; the small-party advantage needs intermediate stakes, few committed voters and high monitoring costs; in high-stakes elections neither party mobilises all its voters

2192.claim: When a German fighter pilot is publicly honoured, the victory rate and death rate of his former peers both rise; reactions are stronger for peers from the same region or who worked closely with him.
2192.treatment_desc: public recognition (a mention in the armed forces' daily bulletin) of a former squadron peer, a non-financial reward creating rivalry and status competition
2192.outcome_desc: monthly aerial victory rate of a German fighter pilot (also monthly death/exit rate, as risk-taking)

magnitudes.outcome: exit (death) risk of former peers after a mention, strictest specification

setting.unit_desc: 5,081 German fighter pilots observed monthly in World War II, 80.9% of whom exit the sample

identification.variation: timing of a public mention of a former peer, comparing peers of mentioned pilots with matched placebo-mention peers before and after
identification.threat: correlated shocks to peers, such as common re-equipment, plane type, front or base; addressed with placebo mentions, plane and squadron fixed effects, and base-distance splits

settled: Individuals care about their relative position (Smith 1759; Veblen 1899; Duesenberry 1949), and many institutions and firms exploit this through prizes and rank-based rewards
Recipients of non-pecuniary rewards show lower absenteeism, greater effort and higher accuracy
contested: Whether recognition raises performance without cost: here it also raises risk-taking and death rates, since every act of recognition lowers the standing of those not recognised
Whether intrinsic rivalry or instrumental motives drive the response: past-peer effects exceed mention-period effects, pointing to intrinsic concerns
gaps: How concerns about relative standing operate in higher-stakes settings, one of several questions the literature leaves open
Whether the findings extend beyond wartime German fighter pilots to other organisations that use non-financial incentives to create status competition
2192.data_asset: newly collected monthly data on confirmed aerial victories and deaths or exits of 5,081 German fighter pilots in World War II, with mentions in the daily bulletin
2192.scope: specific setting of WWII German fighter pilots; peers from the same region or who worked closely with the honoured pilot react more; non-financial rewards crowd in both effort and risk-taking

2316.claim: Microfinance entry cuts social network links, especially among households unlikely to borrow: 22% (0.7pp) fewer low-type links in treated neighbourhoods, with losses in informal borrowing and risk smoothing.
2316.treatment_desc: introduction of microfinance: entry of a microfinance institution across 75 Karnataka villages, and randomised entry across Hyderabad neighbourhoods
2316.outcome_desc: social network links between households (financial and non-financial relationships), by household type (low vs high likelihood of borrowing), including triads

magnitudes.outcome: links among low-type households in treated MF neighbourhoods
links among low-type households in treated MF neighbourhoods
likelihood that a triad of low types dissolves in MF regions

setting.unit_desc: 75 villages in Karnataka (two survey waves) plus neighbourhoods in a Hyderabad RCT; household networks within them

identification.variation: entry of microfinance across 75 villages before and after, with differential trends by village size, replicated in a Hyderabad RCT of microfinance entry across neighbourhoods
identification.threat: village selection into microfinance entry: baseline network characteristics are balanced conditional on village size, with differential-trend robustness checks

settled: Social networks supply credit, insurance, information and advice, substituting for absent or poorly performing formal institutions
Expansion of formal markets changes incentives to maintain relationships, potentially affecting even non-beneficiaries (Arrow 2000; Putnam 2000)
contested: Whether existing network-formation models can explain the loss of links among households unlikely to borrow: they struggle to, which motivates the paper's model
gaps: The forces behind the loss of links after microfinance entry: the model fits the data but is not necessarily the right or only mechanism
2316.data_asset: household network surveys in 75 Karnataka villages and in Hyderabad neighbourhoods, with income, consumption and informal borrowing data in Hyderabad
2316.scope: largest among households unlikely to borrow, even in triangles with no borrower; no greater effect on links involving likely borrowers; replicated in two settings

1380.claim: Domestic survival concerns make limited democracies the most aggressive regime type: dyads of two limited democracies are the most dispute-prone (Correlates of War, 1816-2000), so democracy and peace are non-monotonically related.
1380.treatment_desc: regime type of states and dyads: full democracy, limited democracy or dictatorship (Polity data), with leaders' domestic survival incentives in a game-theoretic model
1380.outcome_desc: probability of a militarized interstate dispute between a pair of countries (dyad), Correlates of War

magnitudes.outcome: conflict probability with a full democracy after dictatorship-to-democracy switc

setting.unit_desc: country dyads classified by regime type with Polity; militarized disputes from Correlates of War

identification.variation: dyad regime-type pairs over time with dyad fixed effects (plus pooled logit and linear probability alternatives), checked against the predictions of a game-theoretic model
identification.threat: results might depend on how limited democracy is defined or on periods of regime change; 24 alternative definitions and subsamples are tried

mechanisms.note: the median voter wants peace but backs aggression against hostile rivals; a full-democracy leader loses median-voter support by attacking a non-hostile country
aggression comes from fear of attack under incomplete information (Schelling's dilemma) plus leaders' survival incentives, giving a non-monotonic regime-peace link

settled: The idea that democracy promotes peace has a long history, from Paine and Kant, and shaped the democratic peace literature and policy
contested: Whether democratization promotes peace: limited democracies are more aggressive than other regimes, including dictatorships, against the simple democratic peace view
gaps: Regime type and conflict after the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989, where dyad-level data with fixed effects are quite limited
1380.data_asset: Polity regime classification into full democracies, limited democracies and dictatorships, merged with Correlates of War militarized disputes, 1816-2000
1380.scope: limited-democracy dyads are most conflict-prone, not only during regime change; full-democracy dyads are peaceful but grow more aggressive in hostile environments; robust to 24 definitions of limited democracy

1567.claim: Primaries are most valuable in one-party-dominant districts: more competitive there, they select high-quality candidates in open seats and punish scandal-hit incumbents (nearly 20% chance of losing in safe districts).
1567.treatment_desc: partisan safety of the constituency: one party's clear advantage in voter loyalties, versus competitive two-party districts
1567.outcome_desc: quality of primary winners and probability that low-quality or scandal-hit incumbents lose the primary, in safe vs competitive districts

magnitudes.outcome: probability (%) a scandal-hit incumbent in a safe district loses the primary, 'n

setting.unit_desc: US House and Senate races and the North Carolina state legislature; about 60% of congressional districts are dominated by one party

identification.variation: cross-district variation in the partisan advantage of the constituency, comparing primary competitiveness and the fate of low-quality or scandal-hit incumbents in safe vs competitive districts
identification.threat: primary vote-share losses may matter little since incumbents win primaries by larger margins than general elections; unclear what information voters have about outcomes

mechanisms.note: primaries in safe, open-seat constituencies select high-quality candidates
primaries punish poor performance, such as scandals, by incumbents of the dominant party

settled: Almost all candidates for major US elected offices are nominated in direct primary elections
Scandals typically hurt incumbents' vote shares (studies of scandals and primary outcomes)
contested: Whether primaries raise politician quality at all: textbooks echo Turner's (1953) verdict that they are not a successful alternative to two-party competition
Whether quality gains from primaries are offset by pulling politicians away from the median voter, as a large literature may suggest
gaps: The full costs and benefits of primaries as an additional hurdle in the electoral process
What information voters actually have about politicians' outcomes and quality when they vote in primaries
1567.data_asset: primary election results and candidate quality indicators (office experience, endorsements, scandals, spending) for US House, Senate and state legislative races
1567.scope: strongest in constituencies dominated by one party and in open-seat races; primaries may also matter in competitive districts when polarization is high

1981.claim: Women from historically more pastoral societies are more likely to have been infibulated, hold stricter norms on promiscuity and have less freedom of mobility; IV supports causality, with male absence as the channel.
1981.treatment_desc: historical dependence on pastoralism of the woman's ancestral ethnic group (Ethnographic Atlas), instrumented by ecological suitability for pastoralism
1981.outcome_desc: infibulation (the most invasive female genital cutting), norms about women's promiscuity, and restrictions on women's freedom of mobility

setting.unit_desc: about 500,000 women from 275 ethnic groups in 34 or 35 countries across Africa, Asia, Europe and South America (abstract and text differ on the count)

identification.variation: within-country variation across women by their ethnic group's historical pastoralism, instrumented by land suitability for pastoralism relative to agriculture
identification.threat: pastoralism may proxy for male dominance, plough use or historical development; tested with plough, non-herding animal husbandry, polygyny and kinship-tightness controls

mechanisms.note: a historical subsistence mode shaped norms that restrict women's sexuality and persist today, through male absence and paternity uncertainty

settled: Anthropologists have long argued that modes of economic production shape societal phenomena such as female status (Boserup 1970; Sanday 1973, 1981; Aberle 1973)
Historical experiences shape present variation in norms and trust (Heldring 2018; Nunn and Wantchekon 2011; Lowes and Montero 2018)
contested: Whether restrictions on women's sexuality stem from male absence under pastoralism, male dominance per se, or historical development; the paper finds male absence
gaps: Why persistence of restrictive norms weakens over time and whether it depends on the persistence of pastoralism itself
1981.data_asset: individual survey data on about 500,000 women linked to ancestral pastoralism (Ethnographic Atlas, 1,202 societies) and land suitability for pastoralism
1981.scope: within-country differences across women of different ethnic ancestry; male absence rather than male dominance or development is the channel; persistence weakens over time (initial evidence)

2043.skip_reason: wrong PDF: slices are only the Online Appendix to Galperti's 'Persuasion: The Art of Changing Worldviews' (proofs of Lemmas 1 and 2 and Figures B1-B2 on concealing); no abstract, introduction or conclusion of the paper itself

1188.claim: Chinese civilization formed through cultural hegemony: an elite bronze-ritual culture centred on ancestral offerings crystallised at Erlitou in the early second millennium BCE and spread by the early Shang.
1188.treatment_desc: an elite ritual culture centred on bronze vessels and ancestral offerings (cultural hegemony) as opposed to dynastic state formation
1188.outcome_desc: formation of Chinese civilization, marked by the spread of bronze vessels with common motifs and ritual forms across the Chinese continental region

setting.unit_desc: archaeological bronze assemblages from Erlitou (Yanshi, Henan) and the Central Plains, early second millennium BCE through the Western Zhou

identification.variation: archaeological and textual analysis of Erlitou bronzes, ritual forms and their spread; no estimated effect
identification.threat: traditional historical texts are largely mythical and there is no contemporaneous written evidence tying Erlitou to the Xia

mechanisms.note: elites of other cultures emulated the offering rites first associated with the Central Plains, anticipating the later common elite culture defined by shared rites

settled: The historicity of the Shang dynasty, or at least its last capital, was confirmed by the 1920s discovery of the Remains of Yin near Anyang
Much of the traditional historical record is mythical in character and unreliable as a basis for historical reconstruction (the author's earlier work)
contested: Whether Erlitou culture represents the Xia dynasty, as many archaeologists take it, given no contemporaneous written evidence
Whether Erlitou was a 'state' (Liu Li and Chen Xingcan 2003) or the origin of a cultural hegemony, as the paper argues
gaps: Whether the Xia, the earliest hereditary dynasty in the records, was historical, an open question since the Shang's historicity was validated
How to match the Xia of the historical records to the archaeological evidence absent contemporaneous written evidence
1188.data_asset: archaeological evidence from Erlitou bronzes with common motifs and ritual forms, later Shang and Zhou bronze assemblages, and traditional historical texts
1188.scope: bronze ritual forms mark an elite culture with continuity from Erlitou to Erligang and from late Shang to Zhou; cultural diversity and local political authority remained

1780.claim: Darwin's reading shifted from early exploitation to later exploration, seeking unusually high cognitive surprise, along a path far more exploratory than the culture's production of books; shifts match epochs of his career.
1780.treatment_desc: stage of Darwin's career: early vs later reading, with shift points detected by an unsupervised Bayesian model
1780.outcome_desc: information-theoretic surprise (KL divergence) of each book relative to the previous book (text-to-text) and to all past reading (text-to-past)

setting.unit_desc: one scholar, Charles Darwin; full text of the books listed in his chronologically organised reading notebooks

identification.variation: topic models (k = 80) of book texts; KL-divergence surprise of each book vs the previous book and vs past reading; compared with a null model and a greedy shortest path

1482.treatment_desc: U.S. food aid shipments (metric tons) to recipient countries, instrumented by lagged U.S. wheat production interacted with a country's propensity to receive U.S. food aid
1482.outcome_desc: incidence of civil conflict (also onset and duration) in a recipient country-year

magnitudes.outcome: incidence of civil conflict per +1,000 MT of U.S. food aid

setting.unit_desc: country-years of U.S. food aid recipient countries; sample mean of about 27,600 MT of food aid and 17.6 percent conflict incidence

identification.variation: year-to-year variation in U.S. wheat production interacted with a country's cross-sectional tendency to receive U.S. food aid
identification.threat: excludability could fail if U.S. wheat production moves foreign conflict through the world price of wheat or of substitute or complement crops

mechanisms.note: larger effects for small-scale conflicts and with poorer transport fit aid being stolen or taxed by small armed groups to fund conflict

settled: Qualitative accounts report that armed groups steal or tax humanitarian aid, with up to eighty percent stolen en route in some reports (Polman and Waters 2010)
Lower agricultural incomes reduce the opportunity cost of fighting and raise conflict (Miguel, Satyanath and Sergenti 2004)
contested: Whether foreign aid raises or lowers conflict: total ODA has no effect globally (Collier and Hoeffler 2002) but within-country total ODA reduces conflict (de Ree and Nillesen 2009)
Whether humanitarian food aid actually promotes conflict, as critics allege, or is merely ineffective
gaps: Effects of food aid at the subnational or project level, which needs finer-grained data
Whether other types of foreign aid affect conflict, since only U.S. food aid is studied
Benefits of food aid, such as lower infant and child mortality, to set against its conflict costs
1482.data_asset: country-year data on U.S. food aid quantities, U.S. wheat production and civil conflict incidence, onset and duration
1482.scope: average effect of U.S. food aid, larger for small-scale conflicts and where transport networks are less developed; not to be extrapolated to foreign aid in general

1684.claim: Globalization exposure (trade, offshoring) raises labour-market risk perceptions and demand for social protection among low-skilled individuals and lowers them among high-skilled ones, in survey data from 16 European countries.

1684.outcome_desc: perceived labour-market risk and preference for social protection / government-led income redistribution, from survey responses

setting.unit_desc: individuals in cross-national survey data from 16 European countries

identification.variation: individuals' skill (education) interacted with exposure to globalization through tradable industry and offshoring
identification.threat: deindustrialisation and ideology could drive risk perceptions and preferences instead, and skill dominates exposure; tested in robustness checks including ideology

settled: Globalization has strong distributional consequences and generates winners and losers
contested: How globalization shapes individuals' perceptions of labour-market risk and policy preferences, on which political economists have no consensus
Whether exposure to international competition affects redistributive preferences at all (Rehm 2009 finds no significant effect)
gaps: How the distributional effects of globalization play out at the macro level
How globalization winners and losers, and their sheltered counterparts, organise politically and get their preferences heard

1684.scope: effects are conditional on skill: with 11 or more years of education exposure lowers redistribution preferences, while for the uneducated it turns positive

1906.claim: American Christians generally see God as young, Caucasian and loving; liberals see God as more feminine, more African American and more loving than conservatives, who see God as older, more intelligent and more powerful.

identification.variation: reverse correlation: participants' choices among noisy face images are aggregated into composite faces for groups such as liberals and conservatives, then rated
identification.threat: denominational information was not collected, and results cannot be generalised beyond American Christians

settled: Views of God are shaped by believers' group-based motivations and cognitive biases
contested: Whether believers see God as the elderly white man of historical depictions, or as younger, Caucasian and loving
Whether religious belief can be treated as a single construct in global measures or primes, given variation within one religion
gaps: Whether views of gods are shaped by believers' own traits and motivations in the same way in other religions and times
Denominational variance in views of God, since denomination was not collected
Variance in views of the divine within other religious traditions that allow visual depictions of gods
Other dimensions of variance in perceptions of God's face, testable with the public data

1906.scope: American Christians only; perceptions vary with ideology and resemble the believer's own attractiveness, age and, less so, race

1915.claim: Interest groups give more campaign money to legislators with higher Bonacich centrality in their social (alumni) network, as a model of competitive vote buying among socially connected legislators predicts.

mechanisms.note: interest groups allocate money in proportion to legislators' Bonacich centralities when legislators are office motivated or numerous

gaps: How past discrimination affects outcomes across generations, for which empirical evidence remains relatively scarce

identification.threat: unobserved differences between controversial and other firms, checked with coefficient stability methods and alternative classifications of controversial sales

dictatorship transferred economic and political power across regimes through firms acting as vehicles

2272.claim: With limited enforcement, optimal incentives are bang-bang and, under a distributional condition, the optimal fiscal rule is a maximally enforced deficit limit that triggers the maximum feasible penalty when violated.

Whether results survive when penalties fall asymmetrically on a principal and an agent
Environments where penalties are not externally enforced but emerge endogenously from strategic play
Multilateral enforcement of a coordinated fiscal rule across a group of countries or regions
2272.scope: the maximally enforced deficit limit needs a distributional condition; violation is optimal only if penalties are weak and high shocks relatively unlikely

1119.claim: In a spatial two-candidate election with a quality advantage and private information on ideology and policy weights, pure-strategy equilibria always exist and approach the earlier mixed equilibrium as policy weights go to zero.

2194.claim: More central Haitian elite families were more likely to take part in the 1991 coup (1 SD of centrality: 9-21 pp), and prices of goods imported by coup families rose differentially under the 2004-2006 autocratic spell.

coup participation probability per 1 SD of centrality (high end)
short-run retail price of coup families' imports, 1 SD more coup share
retail price of coup families' imports with price dynamics, 1 SD more

Whether the VAT is self-enforcing in low-enforcement settings, where buyer and seller reports mismatch massively despite being cross-checkable

mechanisms.note: median voter's location still shifts equilibrium platforms, but Downsian competition yields divergent, more extreme candidates instead of convergence
