1456.claim: Pre-election audit disclosure cuts Puerto Rican municipal corruption by about 67% in the short term, but the effect fades: next-round corruption is no lower, consistent with voters selecting competent but opportunistic mayors.
1456.treatment_desc: municipal government audits made public before the election versus audits that became public only after it, in Puerto Rico
1456.outcome_desc: municipal corruption measured as corrupt violations per audit report, including findings attributed to the mayor or vice-mayor

magnitudes.outcome: municipal corruption level in the audit round after pre-election disclosure (sho

setting.unit_desc: Puerto Rican municipalities over consecutive audit rounds; one analysis sample falls from 326 to 241 municipality-time observations

identification.variation: whether a municipality's audit was released before or after the election, within municipalities over audit rounds with municipality and time fixed effects, interacted with seat competitiveness

mechanisms.note: pre-election audits raise mayors' electoral accountability and cut corruption in the short run, as political agency models predict
no lasting effect on corruption fits voters selecting competent but opportunistic politicians rather than honest ones
in the reputation-building model a mayor with a better reputation exploits information asymmetries to rent-seek, leaving voters indifferent to a challenger

settled: Voters' access to evaluations of politician performance enhances responsiveness, reduces corruption and promotes electoral accountability in the short run, as in field experiments on audits
contested: Whether information dissemination can sustainably cut corruption, which depends on whether voters can tell honest from corrupt politicians or only select competent but opportunistic ones
Whether some politicians are virtuous or all are opportunistic but differ in competence (Fearon 1999; Besley 2005)
Whether corruption is a social norm or habit in low- and middle-income countries or responds strictly to structure (Fisman and Miguel 2007)
gaps: Whether information dissemination policies generate a sustained reduction in rent seeking, which depends on differences among politicians and their dynamic incentives
1456.data_asset: unique longitudinal data on municipal government audits in Puerto Rico, with findings classified as corrupt and matched to election outcomes
1456.scope: the short-run fall is large but in the next audit round the gap between groups is 0.08 violations per report and statistically indistinguishable from zero; the effect varies with the competitiveness of mayoral seats

1761.claim: Policy restrictions lower the returns to political information and can reduce redistribution: in a lab experiment a minimum-transfer restriction lowered offers by 0.11 to 0.35, as generous senders cut their offers.
1761.treatment_desc: an exogenous restriction on the government's policy range, a minimum transfer requirement, framed as an internationally imposed minimum spending requirement, in a lab game
1761.outcome_desc: offer made by the sender (government analogue) to the receiver (voter analogue) in the lab game, on a 0-10 histogram scale; also receivers' acquisition of costly information

magnitudes.outcome: offer, smallest effect of the restriction (threshold 2)
offer, largest effect of the restriction (threshold 3.5)

setting.unit_desc: subjects in a controlled laboratory experiment, an ultimatum game with asymmetric information

identification.variation: comparison of games with and without a minimum-offer restriction, at different thresholds, allowing for sender types

mechanisms.note: restrictions are praised as commitment devices against time inconsistency, but they lower the value of political information and so voters' incentives to be informed
a fiscal restriction may cut redistribution by lowering poorer voters' acquisition of political information

settled: Institutional restrictions are commended as solutions to time inconsistency, generating credible commitments (Kydland and Prescott)
Rational voters acquire political information only while its marginal benefit exceeds its marginal cost
contested: Whether restricting government policy options is desirable, given that the rules-versus-discretion literature has long ignored the advantages of fully empowered governments
gaps: The unintended consequences of policy restrictions for voter information and participation, which current research has largely ignored
Whether the information-incentive mechanism applies beyond internationally imposed minimum spending requirements
1761.data_asset: controlled laboratory experiment data on offers and information acquisition
1761.scope: average effect on offers is negative, but selfish senders are forced to raise offers and genuinely altruistic senders are unaffected; lab evidence, and the authors do not claim restrictions are always bad

1910.skip_reason: wrong PDF: slices are the 5-page supplemental appendix of Buisseret and Prato (bounds on vote shares and the proof of Proposition 1), not the paper itself

1956.skip_reason: wrong PDF: slices are an Indonesian-language article on Islamic values in Indonesian foreign policy toward the Iran-Israel conflict (Rahmatullah and Siregar), not Stutzer et al. on ballot propositions

2176.claim: In a model of electoral competition with targetable intervention, a relative electoral sensitivity effect can make majoritarian systems allocate resources more equally than PR, against the conventional wisdom.
2176.treatment_desc: majoritarian versus proportional representation electoral system, in a model of electoral competition with targetable government intervention and heterogeneous localities
2176.outcome_desc: no empirical outcome; modelled inequality in government interventions across localities (equilibrium allocations compared with Atkinson dominance)

setting.unit_desc: theoretical model with heterogeneous localities grouped into districts; no data

identification.variation: equilibrium allocations of a model with probabilistic voting compared under majoritarian and proportional systems, where the geographic distribution of votes matters more in majoritarian systems

mechanisms.note: swing-voter targeting holds, but in majoritarian systems the electoral sensitivity of other voters in a district can push parties to spread resources more equally

settled: Geographic inequalities in public goods, services and taxation are substantial (Alesina, Baqir and Easterly 1999; Banerjee, Iyer and Somanathan 2008; Albouy 2009)
Political factors such as apportionment, district contestability, turnout, information and core supporters shape distributive politics (e.g., Ansolabehere, Gerber and Snyder 2002; Stromberg 2008)
Political distortions of government interventions are substantial: about 25 percent of public funds allocated by Brazilian legislators are distorted (Finan and Mazzocco 2016)
contested: Whether government interventions are more unequal under majoritarian than proportional systems, as the recurrent view holds because parties target a smaller fraction of voters under majoritarian rules
gaps: Empirical studies of sub-district allocation in majoritarian systems should control for other voter groups' electoral sensitivity; the empirical literature remains to be revisited
2176.scope: the effect depends on the geographic distribution of voters and can be strong enough to make inequality lower under majoritarian than PR systems, not always

2178.claim: In a Sierra Leone infrastructure grants competition, nudging delegation to higher-skill individuals beat chiefly control (technocrats +0.50 SD on proposal quality); attempts to boost participation were largely ineffective.
2178.treatment_desc: randomised public nudge to delegate project choice to higher-skill community members, with or without management training, versus default chiefly control, crossed with participation-boosting community-driven development treatments
2178.outcome_desc: quality of village infrastructure grant proposals, an index of three expert evaluations, in a real grants competition

magnitudes.outcome: proposal quality index, selected and trained technocrats vs chiefs (Arm 3 vs Arm
proposal quality index, treatment-on-the-treated effect of delegating project ch

setting.unit_desc: villages entering a real-world infrastructure grants competition; 98 percent of villages entered

identification.variation: random assignment of villages to six arms combining a delegation-to-skill nudge, management training and participation-boosting community-driven development, against chiefly control
identification.threat: missing proposal scores, handled with imputation bounds that change the estimates little; one specification deviates from the pre-analysis plan to control for the participation treatment

mechanisms.note: who decides matters: higher-skill decision-makers produce better proposals than chiefs
skill rather than broader participation was the binding constraint on local development outcomes

settled: Where the state is weak, traditional authorities control local public goods provision and are typically older, less educated and exclusionary in rule
contested: Whether encouraging delegation to higher-skill individuals or broader inclusion, alone or combined, improves local development decisions
Whether recruiting higher-skill individuals broadens participation or only shifts power to another, still overwhelmingly male, educated local elite
gaps: Why communities do not seek out technically competent managers on their own to improve their chances of winning outside funds
2178.data_asset: real-world infrastructure grants competition in Sierra Leone with expert evaluations of proposal quality across six experimental arms
2178.scope: compliance with delegation was partial, so the treatment-on-the-treated effect is about 1 SD; participation-boosting was largely ineffective; offered as a low-cost option where local democratization is infeasible

2255.claim: Interest-group coalitions opposing US trade agreements are mainly progressive (environment, human rights, economic justice) with labor allies; right-wing populist groups are largely absent (5,906 groups).
2255.treatment_desc: ideological motive behind interest-group mobilisation against US trade policy: populism, worker protectionism or progressive fair-trade demands
2255.outcome_desc: participation of nonbusiness groups, 5,906 unique groups, in organised coalitions opposing US trade agreements and globalisation, by group type, issue and letter content

magnitudes.outcome: percent share of nonbusiness group lobbying on trade by groups in anti-trade coa
percent share of nonbusiness group PAC contributions by groups in anti-trade coa

setting.unit_desc: 5,906 unique nonbusiness interest groups that joined coalitions opposing US trade agreements and globalisation

identification.variation: descriptive analysis of original data on group types in coalitions, activation across trade issues, the topical content of coalition letters and union motives; no estimated effect

mechanisms.note: union opposition reflects sincere progressive motives alongside the classic search for protection, and the wider coalition is progressive rather than protectionist

settled: Trade politics is a classic site for the influence of special interests
Sincere support for causes operates alongside the search for protection in trade opposition (Ahlquist and Levi 2013; Ahlquist, Clayton and Levi 2014)
contested: Which anti-globalization ideology, populism, worker protectionism or progressive fair trade, drives interest-group mobilisation against trade, which was unclear among nonbusiness groups
Whether the populist backlash against globalization is durable, given the absence of right-wing interest groups organised around trade
gaps: Why progressive groups have been so successful in anti-trade mobilisation, and whether it matters
Differences in organisational duration across anti-trade coalitions
Whether right-wing interest groups or the Republican party will take up populist opposition to trade
2255.data_asset: original data on 5,906 nonbusiness groups' participation in anti-trade coalitions, with coalition letters and lobbying and PAC contributions
2255.scope: US trade politics and nonbusiness groups; progressive-labor alliance dominates while right-wing populist interest-group opposition is largely absent; union participation reflects both progressive and protectionist motives

2270.claim: Foreign countries whose agents meet US legislators more receive more US aid, and their firms' US subsidiaries more corporate subsidies; costs to legislators are negligible.
2270.treatment_desc: in-person meetings between foreign-government agents and US legislators, governors and agency employees from DOJ filings, with legislator deaths as an exogenous shock to connections
2270.outcome_desc: foreign aid and financial assistance received by the lobbying country, and corporate subsidies to US subsidiaries of firms headquartered in connected countries

magnitudes.outcome: likelihood of corporate subsidies for US subsidiaries of firms from connected co
amount of corporate subsidies for US subsidiaries of firms from connected countr

setting.unit_desc: foreign country-year panels built from over 230,000 date-stamped meetings of foreign agents with US legislators, governors and executive agency employees

identification.variation: within-country changes in the number of meetings with country and year fixed effects for aid, and legislator deaths as exogenous shocks to connections for corporate subsidies
identification.threat: meetings may reflect short-term quid pro quo or reverse causation rather than influence; the authors note that connections persist after legislators leave powerful committees and call the estimates first-order quantification

mechanisms.note: access gained through meetings is followed by more aid and subsidies for the lobbying country and its firms, with little electoral cost to legislators

settled: Foreign governments spend billions of dollars on Washington lobbyists to shape US policy, with cases such as Ethiopia's aid and Saudi arms sales
contested: Whether foreign lobbying influences US policy, given intense public debate but no solid evidence until now
Whether meetings reflect short-term quid pro quo or lasting connections, since agents keep ties after legislators leave powerful committees
gaps: How much sway foreign nations have over US policy and what benefits politicians gain from supporting them
Which theoretical models of lobbying best fit the new data on meetings
2270.data_asset: novel dataset of over 230,000 date-stamped in-person meetings between foreign agents and US legislators, governors and agency staff from Department of Justice filings, 2000-2018
2270.scope: US federal and state officials, 2000-2018; foreign agents meet disproportionately legislators on committees important for aid and subsidies; costs to legislators are on average negligible

2339.claim: France's 1995 ban on firm donations made candidates advertise their local presence and economic issues less, and led candidates from nonmainstream parties to use more extreme language (difference-in-differences).
2339.treatment_desc: France's 1995 national ban on firm donations to candidates, with exposure measured by a candidate's pre-ban (1993) firm donations
2339.outcome_desc: content of candidates' campaign manifestos: references to local presence (a local index), economic issues, and extreme language

setting.unit_desc: candidates in French parliamentary elections before (1993) and after (1997) the ban, with their campaign manifestos and contributions

identification.variation: pre-ban firm donations interacted with the post-ban period, with candidate fixed effects and party-by-time effects
identification.threat: firm donations are not randomly allocated across candidates, so the causal effect needs an identification strategy that handles this

mechanisms.note: private donors shape politicians' topics of interest, so removing firm money changes what candidates talk about

settled: Firms expect returns on their campaign donations (Bombardini and Trebbi 2011; Boas, Hidalgo and Richardson 2014)
contested: Whether campaign contributions shape what candidates say and not only electoral results, which prior work mostly studied
gaps: How campaign finance reforms change the information available to voters through candidates' rhetoric
2339.data_asset: novel dataset combining campaign manifestos of candidates in French parliamentary elections with their campaign contributions
2339.scope: the effect on more extreme language appears among candidates from nonmainstream parties; French legislative candidates, 1993 versus 1997

2364.claim: The onset of wheat harvest, a transitory anticipated rise in labor demand, reduces insurgent attacks by 6-21% in Afghanistan, Iraq and Pakistan, consistent with an opportunity-cost mechanism.
2364.treatment_desc: onset of the wheat harvest, a transitory and anticipated rise in labor demand, interacted with each district's wheat production intensity
2364.outcome_desc: monthly number or share of insurgent attacks in a district, from Iraq Body Count, US military SIGACTS and local media datasets

magnitudes.outcome: monthly attacks in high-intensity districts at mean wheat cultivation, Iraq, low
monthly attacks in high-intensity districts at mean wheat cultivation, Iraq, hig
monthly attacks in high-intensity districts at mean wheat cultivation, Pakistan
monthly attacks in high-intensity districts at mean wheat cultivation, Afghanist

setting.unit_desc: district-months: Iraq 2004-2009, Pakistan 2002-2010, Afghanistan 2004-2014

identification.variation: exogenous timing of harvest by month interacted with district wheat production intensity, with district-by-year and month-by-year fixed effects
identification.threat: separating opportunity costs from other determinants of conflict such as temperature and rainfall, and fighting that shifts to adjacent months; checked with controls and dynamic specifications

mechanisms.note: higher returns to work at harvest lower the relative return to fighting, so attacks fall; opportunity cost matters even in highly ideological insurgencies

settled: Low per capita income is the best predictor of civil war (Fearon and Laitin 2003), so poverty and poor employment prospects are widely seen as drivers of conflict (World Bank 2011)
Theory links the availability and rewards of work to the onset and intensity of conflict, the opportunity cost mechanism (Becker 1968; Dal Bo and Dal Bo 2011; Grossman 1991)
contested: Whether higher returns to labor lower conflict: opportunity cost is hard to separate from other determinants, and price rises for labor-intensive crops can increase conflict (Crost and Felter 2020)
Whether opportunity costs matter in settings with highly ideological insurgencies, where the paper finds they do
gaps: Whether harvest-driven falls in conflict appear in other conflict settings beyond Afghanistan, Iraq and Pakistan
2364.data_asset: monthly district conflict data from US military records, Iraq Body Count and local media reports, matched to wheat cultivation and harvest calendars
2364.scope: evaluated at mean wheat cultivation intensity in districts with conflict; less significant in the full Pakistan sample, where most districts see no recorded conflict; dynamic estimates show a fall at harvest, not a shift to adjacent months

2375.claim: Sectors and commodities more exposed to foreign political risk innovate more (US sectors, a global sample, critical minerals), especially when risk comes from geopolitical adversaries, which lowers reliance on risky imports.
2375.treatment_desc: time-varying sector-level exposure to foreign political risk, built from each sector's import sources weighted by country political risk (ICRG), a threat to access to foreign inputs
2375.outcome_desc: innovative activity measured as log patents per sector-year in US sectors, mineral-specific patents for critical minerals, and country-sector patents in a global sample

setting.unit_desc: US sector-years, country-sector-years in a global sample, and critical minerals; trade policy data from Global Trade Alert since 2008

identification.variation: within-sector changes over time in exposure to foreign political risk, with sector and year fixed effects, decennial estimates and pre-trend checks
identification.threat: import patterns may respond to political risk exposure; addressed with a falsification test using export-weighted exposure and pre-trend checks

settled: Scarcity or necessity can drive invention (e.g., Popp 2002; Acemoglu 2010; Hanlon 2015; Moscona and Sastry 2023)
contested: Whether directed innovation helps or hurts: it cuts reliance on risky suppliers but weakens the export performance of countries in political turmoil
gaps: Models of geopolitics that integrate interactions between innovation and policy
How firms and countries react in practice to foreign threats to production, and whether this mediates the economic impact of political turmoil
2375.data_asset: sector-level patent data combined with time-varying industry exposure to foreign political risk, trade flows and Global Trade Alert policy data
2375.scope: the response is strongest when risk emanates from geopolitical adversaries; holds in US sectors, a global country-sector sample and critical minerals; exports fall more for country-sectors that sell to innovation-intensive markets

1537.claim: In 18 OECD countries (1970-2006), the median voter hypothesis (Meltzer-Richard) and power resources theory are jointly relevant for redistribution and inequality; they are not mutually exclusive.
1537.treatment_desc: bias in the initial market income distribution (median-voter channel) together with left partisanship, union density and corporatism (power resources)
1537.outcome_desc: redistribution measured as the reduction in income inequality, market wage inequality and disposable income inequality, in a three-stage model of inequality formation

setting.unit_desc: panel of 18 OECD countries; Austria and Greece are dropped from one hypothesis test for missing data

identification.variation: cross-national panel of 18 OECD countries estimating a composite model of wage inequality, redistribution and power resources, with interactions between left partisanship and corporatism
identification.threat: the direct and indirect effects of the median voter cannot be estimated accurately without simultaneously modelling power resources, and vice versa

mechanisms.note: greater redistribution goes with a more biased initial income distribution as Meltzer-Richard predicts, but the effect is mis-estimated without power resources
union density and centralization shape wage distribution, and the effect of left partisanship depends on corporatism

settled: Left-wing party strength raises welfare effort (Cameron 1978; Stephens 1979)
Union density and centralization strongly affect wage dispersion (Wallerstein 1999)
Democracy lowers labor's cost of participation and freedom of association lets workers accumulate power resources (Schumpeter 1942; Rodrik 1998)
contested: Whether the median voter hypothesis and power resources theory conflict: they are thought to have contrasting predictions, but the paper shows they are not mutually exclusive
Whether left parties reduce inequality without wage-bargaining coordination (Beramendi and Cusack 2009), and whether corporatism constrains or facilitates left partisanship (Rueda 2008)
1537.data_asset: panel of 18 OECD countries, 1970-2006, on market wage inequality, redistribution, left partisanship, union density and corporatism
1537.scope: 18 OECD democracies in 1970-2006; the effect of left partisanship depends on corporatism

2001.claim: A principal cannot induce much agent effort on a problem whose resolution burdens the agent and erodes its future leverage; repeated-game enforcement breaks down and the problem persists.
2001.treatment_desc: a principal's attempt to induce an agent to resolve a problem whose resolution creates an ongoing cost for the agent and reduces the agent's ability to impose future costs on the principal
2001.outcome_desc: no empirical outcome; modelled level of agent effort the principal can induce and the expected duration of the problem

setting.unit_desc: formal repeated principal-agent model; motivating cases include US security assistance to Pakistan in 2018, counterinsurgency, proxy wars and arms control

identification.variation: repeated-game principal-agent model in which the agent's power to punish the principal depends on the problem staying unresolved

mechanisms.note: repeated-game enforcement of commitments breaks down when resolving the problem would remove the agent's future leverage
principal-agent effort inducement with moral hazard and limited commitment is extended by an incentive problem tied to the agent's future leverage

settled: Principal-agent work on counterinsurgency, client states, aid and proxy wars stresses diverging interests, moral hazard and limited credible commitment enforced by threats of future punishment
contested: Whether a principal can induce agent effort through repeated-game threats when resolving the problem would remove the agent's leverage; the paper says it cannot
2001.scope: induced effort is very small and the problem very long-lived when actors are patient, yet the principal still prefers working through the agent; for arms control it gives an upper bound on feasible breakout periods

2060.claim: In a model where numbers favour the common people and knowledge the elite, competition can leave the majority behind, inviting anti-elite entry and parties that follow popular opinion over experts.
2060.treatment_desc: electoral competition between parties with signals about the state, where the common people hold a numbers advantage and the elite a knowledge advantage, including entry of an anti-elite party
2060.outcome_desc: no empirical outcome; modelled party platforms catering to the elite, entry of an anti-elite party, and parties following popular opinion rather than experts

setting.unit_desc: formal model of electoral competition with two voter groups, the common people and the elite, and party signals; extended to a three-party system

identification.variation: electoral competition model in which groups differ in numbers and knowledge, with extensions for anti-elite entry and three-party competition

mechanisms.note: numbers favour the majority but knowledge favours the elite, so competition can cater to the elite and leave a majority behind
parties may pander by following popular opinion even when the common people would gain from parties relying on experts

settled: Populists claim to defend the common people against the elite and stress the wisdom of the people over expert advice (Rodrik 2018)
Voters have grown disappointed with traditional politicians and parties in recent decades (Stiglitz 2002; Acemoglu et al. 2013; Algan et al. 2017; Rodrik 2018)
contested: What drives populism: globalization, automation and the financial-crisis recession (Guriev and Papaioannou 2020; Noury and Roland 2020), versus a left-behind majority created by electoral competition
gaps: Whether the electoral bias towards the elite is reinforced when compensation is feasible
Whether populist policies are provided by traditional parties or by newcomers when earlier platforms carry information about what is good for the common people
2060.scope: results depend on the quality of party signals; better-informed traditional parties can raise the common people's suspicion

2311.claim: In East German emigration applications, active opposition to the regime raised the chance of exit approval but also of punishment for applying; pensioners were more likely to secure exit and professionals less likely.
2311.treatment_desc: applicant's active opposition to the regime, along with age and occupation, as recorded in East German emigration application files
2311.outcome_desc: approval of an emigration application by the East German state, and punishment of the applicant for applying

setting.unit_desc: applicants whose declassified emigration applications, over 20,000 pages, were coded from East Germany's state archives

identification.variation: individual-level variation across applicants in coded opposition activity, age and occupation, regressed on the regime's approval and punishment decisions

settled: Exit reduces the ranks of dissidents exercising voice, in the exit-versus-voice framework
Autocracies use exit visas, no-travel lists, passport controls and labor agreements to let some citizens leave while forcing others to stay
contested: Whether autocracies set exit costs strategically to target opponents, rather than uniformly as the exit-versus-voice framework typically assumes
Who applies and is denied emigration, since earlier studies examined only the characteristics of successful emigrants
gaps: The strategic mix of co-optation, repression and emigration policy in autocracies
How state capacity affects the adoption and effectiveness of selective emigration policies
How autocracies such as China and Russia have used the targeted safety valve and how it has evolved over time
2311.data_asset: original dataset coded from over 20,000 pages of declassified emigration applications in East Germany's state archives
2311.scope: East Germany only; the opposition effect is larger in later applications; pensioners more likely and professionals less likely to secure exit, consistent with economic-cost considerations

2351.claim: Kinshasa's traffic police run a coalition extortion scheme of agents, managers and judicial police: real revenue is five times fine revenue, and an experiment suggests the vehicle quota subverts service.
2351.treatment_desc: the traffic police agency's vehicle quota extortion scheme, tested with a randomised encouragement for station managers to reduce the quota, stratified by team and day
2351.outcome_desc: traffic police service delivery in the experiment, such as whether pull-overs target real infractions; the outcome variables and their signs are not visible in the slices

magnitudes.outcome: agency's real revenue relative to revenue from fines
percent share of agents' total income from bribes net of payments to superiors
percent share of station police staff's total income from bribes net of payments
percent share of observed street pull-overs with proof of an infraction

setting.unit_desc: Kinshasa traffic police agents and stations; the experiment, designed in 2015, covers 7 of 14 stations in one battalion plus the central station

identification.variation: randomised encouragement for the station manager to reduce the quota, stratified within team and day blocks, with effects estimated for compliers
identification.threat: imbalance across arms, reduced by stratifying the randomisation into 30 strata; estimates apply to compliers with the encouragement

mechanisms.note: coalitions of agents, managers and judicial police extort drivers, with revenue far above official fines and agents free to fabricate infractions
corruption is a scheme run through the hierarchy, not just the discretion of an individual official, and managers take part

settled: Corruption by state officials with discretion is socially costly (Shleifer and Vishny 1993; Bardhan 1997; Olken and Pande 2012)
Corruption can be organised as a scheme within an agency, as in Wade's study of irrigation canals in India (Wade 1982)
contested: Whether corruption is mainly the problem of individual officials with discretion or of coalitions with their managers, and whether such schemes signal state weakness
Whether state weakness explains corruption, given that coalitions of officials can yield large illicit revenue
gaps: The players, strategies and equilibria of the broader hierarchy of payments to higher-ups in which the scheme sits
How prevalent such schemes are beyond the public scandals for which evidence exists
2351.data_asset: original multi-branch data collection in Kinshasa's traffic police, with observers, escorted drivers, revenue and income data and a randomised encouragement experiment
2351.scope: one agency in Kinshasa; the authors say the logic is widespread; the experiment covers part of one battalion and effects are for compliers; revenue is mostly unofficial

2442.claim: In a survey of 20,400 US residents, zero-sum thinking predicts support for redistribution, affirmative action and restrictive immigration, and is linked to ancestors' mobility, immigration and enslavement.
2442.treatment_desc: zero-sum thinking: the belief that gains for one person or group come at the expense of others, measured by a survey index across several domains
2442.outcome_desc: support for redistribution from the rich to the poor, affirmative action for women and Black Americans, and restrictive immigration policies, from survey policy views

setting.unit_desc: survey of about 20,400 US residents with information on ancestors; generality checked with World Values Survey data from 72 countries

identification.variation: cross-sectional variation in a zero-sum index across respondents, related to policy views and to ancestors' mobility, immigration and enslavement, with controls and a Gelbach decomposition
identification.threat: the zero-sum index might proxy other values and beliefs that matter for policy views; checked with controls for core beliefs and ideology and indices that drop the most similar domain

mechanisms.note: ancestors' experiences of mobility, immigration and enslavement shape zero-sum thinking directly and through local exposure, as cultural transmission across generations

settled: Zero-sum perceptions, Foster's image of limited good, have been prevalent throughout history, from mercantilism to modern trade and immigration policies (Foster 1965, 1967; Thurow 1980; Rubin 2003)
contested: Whether Foster's image of limited good, developed for rural Mexico, applies generally to modern societies such as the US (Bergeron et al. 2023)
Whether zero-sum thinking is a partisan issue: the paper finds it mainly explains within-party variation in policy views
gaps: Implications of zero-sum thinking for new party formation, coalitions and electoral platforms
Whether shorter-run experiences during an individual's own life also affect zero-sum thinking
2442.data_asset: new survey of about 20,400 US residents measuring zero-sum thinking, political views and ancestors' characteristics, plus World Values Survey data for 72 countries
2442.scope: US residents; zero-sum thinking explains within-party variation more than partisanship; three factors, intergenerational mobility, immigration and enslavement, predict it, directly and through county exposure

1367.claim: Economic history underweights developing regions (under 20% of Journal of Economic History submissions in 2004-08 lay outside the West), so a forum on their institutions, path dependence and growth is needed.
1367.treatment_desc: historical institutions, path dependence and colonial rule as determinants of long-run development in Africa, Asia, Latin America and the Middle East (editorial survey)
1367.outcome_desc: long-term economic development and growth retardation across developing regions; no estimated outcome

setting.unit_desc: editorial survey of research on Africa, China, India, Latin America and the Middle East; Table 1 counts Journal of Economic History submissions by region for 2004-2008

identification.variation: editorial survey of regional literatures with a table of journal submissions by region; no estimated effect

settled: Studies of developing regions have deepened understanding of the longevity of institutions, the roles of trade and education in growth, and the consequences of colonialism
Better estimation techniques and richer data have shifted work on historical persistence from possibly spurious correlations toward better identification (Nunn 2009)
contested: The net macro effect of colonial rule in India, which needs detailed micro-studies
What explains growth retardation in developing regions and when a region stops being developing, given widely diverging twentieth-century development paths
gaps: How institutions, path dependency, technological change and evolutionary processes shape economic growth in developing regions, given the dominance of research on the North
Many valuable data sets and historical episodes relating to developing regions remain unexplored
1367.data_asset: counts of Journal of Economic History submissions by region, 2004-2008
1367.scope: regional surveys of Africa, China, India, Latin America and the Middle East; themes judged suited to South-South comparison

1373.claim: Democracy has a positive, significant impact on the adoption of economic reforms across 150 countries in 1960-2004 (full democracy raises the reform index by 0.22 in the long run); no evidence that reforms foster democracy.
1373.treatment_desc: level of democracy in a country-year, with instruments based on democracy in political allies and neighbours
1373.outcome_desc: index of economic reforms normalised between 0 and 1, covering financial, capital and banking sectors, product markets, agriculture and trade

magnitudes.outcome: economic reform index (0-1), long-run effect of moving to complete democracy

setting.unit_desc: country-year panel of reforms in 150 countries

identification.variation: country and reform fixed effects with interactions between country and reform characteristics and global reform waves, plus instrumenting democracy with democracy in political allies and neighbours
identification.threat: reverse causality and omitted variables such as income, bureaucratic quality, education and political stability; addressed with controls, instruments and tests of feedback from reforms to democracy

settled: Many reforms and take-offs happened under dictatorships, such as Chile under Pinochet, South Korea under Park, East Asian economies and most contemporary industrialised countries
contested: Whether democracy hinders or facilitates economic reforms, since strong theoretical arguments run both ways, such as capture by interest groups versus benevolent dictators

gaps: Evidence on the democracy-reform relationship across many reforms, countries and years, which data limitations have restricted
1373.data_asset: novel dataset on economic reforms in financial, capital and banking sectors, product markets, agriculture and trade for 150 countries, 1960-2004, the most exhaustive in the literature
1373.scope: broad set of reforms over 1960-2004; robustness checks restrict the sample to communist and developing countries; hyperinflation episodes lower the probability of reform only weakly

2305.claim: Rwanda's high state capacity rests on state-society networks from the historical state's expansion, uncorrelated with Weberian capacity; longer historical state presence predicts rule-following today, Weberian capacity does not.
2305.treatment_desc: years of historical state presence under the pre-colonial Nyiginya kingdom's segmentary state, a proxy for the strength of state-society networks
2305.outcome_desc: rule compliance: following an unenforced rule in a laboratory exercise in rural Rwanda; also Weberian state capacity measures in 1980 such as fiscal capacity and local government outcomes

2936.claim: State governing parties skew transfers to counties toward their strongest supporters (1957-97) with only weak evidence of targeting pivotal counties; more spending raises later turnout, i.e. mobilization rather than conversion.
2936.treatment_desc: party control of state government interacted with a county's traditional vote share for the governing party (including changes in party control)

identification.variation: changes in state party control over time interacted with counties' traditional support for the governing party, with county-clustered errors
identification.threat: state spending depends on many factors other than partisanship and party control, so raw comparisons are suggestive but not definitive

mechanisms.note: little or no support for targeting areas with many swing voters, contrary to Lindbeck-Weibull and Dixit-Londregan; evidence instead fits party loyalist targeting

settled: The swing voter model is by far the most common model of party electoral strategy in political economy today (Lindbeck & Weibull; Dixit & Londregan)
contested: Whether parties target pivotal swing areas or reward their strongest supporters (the paper finds loyalists, not swing areas, get more)
Whether party control affects state expenditures at all: earlier studies, e.g. Jennings (1979) and Dye (1984), find mixed results
gaps: Models of distributive politics in which government spending affects turnout, which swing-voter models assume away

2864.claim: With a favored candidate in a Downsian model, pure equilibria often fail; in the mixed equilibrium the favored candidate locates more centrally and wins with probability above 0.5, nearing the median as the advantage vanishes.
2864.treatment_desc: a fixed non-policy advantage (e.g. charisma) of one candidate valued by all voters, in a two-candidate one-dimensional Downsian election
2864.outcome_desc: equilibrium candidate locations in the policy space and each candidate's probability of winning

identification.variation: equilibrium analysis of a simultaneous location game in which candidates maximize the probability of victory, with a discrete policy space for the main results
identification.threat: payoff discontinuities in the continuous location game force a discrete policy space; the continuous-location mixed equilibrium is not solved

mechanisms.note: for any positive advantage candidates diverge and pure equilibria vanish, yet the Downsian median-voter outcome remains a good approximation when the advantage is small

settled: Simple spatial (Downsian) models are the tool of choice for studying candidate competition in mass elections
With no uncertainty about the median voter, the advantaged candidate wins with probability 1 (Ansolabehere & Snyder)
contested: Whether the standard Downsian median-voter result is a knife-edge case once candidates differ in non-policy advantage (the paper finds it is a good approximation when the advantage is small)
gaps: The mixed equilibrium of the game with continuous candidate locations, a natural next step
Whether the results hold for non-uniform distributions of the median voter's ideal point, as examples suggest
2864.scope: two candidates, one policy dimension, one advantage valued by all voters; main results use a discrete policy space and a uniform median-voter distribution, with examples suggesting wider validity

2876.claim: Higher pay in office lowers the average quality of entrants to politics and turnover in office, with ambiguous effects on career politicians' quality; a higher market wage raises entrant quality and turnover.

settled: Many US House members leave office voluntarily: of post-1945 entrants who left alive by 1994, 46% left voluntarily and 39% of those took private-sector jobs (Diermeier, Keane & Merlo 2005)
A first term in Congress raises post-congressional private-sector wages, but additional congressional experience adds little (Diermeier, Keane & Merlo 2005)
contested: Whether higher pay in office raises or lowers the quality of career politicians, which the model leaves ambiguous
gaps: Empirical analysis of politicians' career paths using the model's implications, e.g. politicians with voluntary careers earning more than those who leave the market sector after defeat

earmarks, unrepresented universities, per 1% rise in lobbying
earmarks, effect of HAC representation (SAC is 34)

identification.threat: endogeneity of lobbying expenditure to expected earmarks; in many specifications the return for unrepresented universities is not statistically different from zero

mechanisms.note: groups aligned with powerful legislators who can cheaply deliver policy lobby less; consistent with informational lobbying (Grossman & Helpman) and agenda-setter models (Helpman & Persson)
HAC and SAC members send earmarks to their districts even in the absence of lobbying

settled: Federal lobbying spending in the US is nearly $2 billion a year and is a main channel for special interests to influence policy (Groseclose, Milyo & Primo 2000)
Representation on appropriations committees increases a district's earmarks (Payne 2003; Savage 1999; Balla et al. 2002)
contested: Whether lobbying itself raises earmarks or well-represented universities receive them regardless, since committee members deliver earmarks without lobbying

3005.scope: academic earmarks only; large returns require representation on the House or Senate Appropriations Committee, with little or no return otherwise

2952.outcome_desc: annual growth rate of real per capita GDP (percent per year); also growth in per capita tax revenues as extractive capacity

annual real per capita GDP growth, centralised vs fragmented, high estimate
long-run per capita GDP growth, centralised regimes (dynamic panel, low end)

mechanisms.note: greater capacity to extract tax revenue is one mechanism through which fiscal centralisation, and to some extent limited government, improved growth

Post-1960 democratic transitions were associated with about a 1% rise in annual real per capita GDP growth (Papaioannou & Siourounis 2008)
contested: Whether limited government raises economic performance directly (no significant direct relationship found, but large interaction effects with fiscal centralisation)
Whether fiscal centralisation or limited government was the more consequential political change in Europe from the Old Regime to World War I
gaps: The main non-fiscal mechanisms through which fiscal centralisation raised growth
Causal evidence on state capacity and long-run growth, since these estimates are not causal
2952.data_asset: new database of fiscal centralisation and limited-government dates with per capita GDP and tax revenues for 11 European countries over four centuries
2952.scope: 11 European countries from the Old Regime to World War I; fiscal centralisation, not limited government, carries the direct growth association; extractive capacity explains 42-58% of the England-France growth gap

3025.claim: In the new GREG georeferenced dataset of ethnic groups, groups with a single territorial cluster face a significantly higher risk of conflict onset; raising clusters from 1 to the mean 6.86 cuts predicted probability by about 20%.

Whether the focus on linguistic boundaries limits the use of ethnic-group territory data for political science questions

2785.claim: In Pakistan, turnover taxes cut corporate evasion by up to 60-70% of corporate income versus profit taxes; a calibrated model has a switch to turnover taxation raising revenue 74% with no loss of aggregate profits.
2785.treatment_desc: taxing firms on turnover rather than profits, via a minimum tax scheme where the larger of the two liabilities applies
2785.outcome_desc: corporate tax evasion as a share of corporate income, from bunching in reported profit rates at the profit/turnover tax kink; corporate tax revenue in the calibrated model

magnitudes.outcome: evasion, % of corporate income, turnover vs profit tax (low end)
evasion, % of corporate income, turnover vs profit tax (high end)
corporate tax revenue, switch to turnover taxation (calibrated model)

setting.unit_desc: universe of corporate tax returns, limited to firms reporting both profit and turnover; number of firms not in slices

identification.variation: bunching in reported profit rates at the kink where the minimum tax switches between turnover and profit taxes
identification.threat: filing responses at the kink mistaken for evasion; checked with empirical measures of N (section 5.3), which show no response to the kink

settled: Tax systems should keep full production efficiency even in second-best settings (Diamond & Mirrlees 1971), a result influential in advice to developing countries
If some commodity cannot be taxed and pure profits are taxed below 100%, some production inefficiency becomes desirable
contested: Whether production-efficient tax systems suit developing countries with limited tax capacity and evasion (the paper argues revenue efficiency can justify production inefficiency)
gaps: Empirical evidence on the trade-off between production and revenue efficiency in choosing tax instruments, which the paper calls virtually absent
Estimates of the additional parameters needed for the general equilibrium analysis of the tax base, which the paper does not estimate

2785.scope: corporate taxpayers in Pakistan where firms pay the larger of turnover and profit liabilities; the best tax base lies between pure profit and pure turnover taxation in general

2727.claim: In a political agency model, term limits can raise voters' ex ante welfare despite weakening accountability: lower office value induces truthful incumbent behaviour, enabling better selection of second-term incumbents.
2727.treatment_desc: term limits that cap the number of terms a politician can serve, in a political agency model

setting.unit_desc: stylised representative democracy with a voter, incumbents of heterogeneous type and challengers

identification.variation: equilibrium analysis of a political agency game with and without term limits, comparing the voter's ex ante utility across equilibria

mechanisms.note: elections discipline incumbents, but reducing the value of office via term limits can still help voters
truthful incumbent behaviour allows voters to retain higher-quality agents for a second term
lower office value makes incumbents stop pooling and implement policies closer to their private preferences

settled: Elections hold politicians accountable through two channels: selective retention of good incumbents and discipline on opportunistic behaviour
Re-election rules chosen by rational voters need not be optimal for them because voters cannot pre-commit to use elections as an incentive (Besley & Smart 2006)
contested: Whether term limits are counterproductive because they weaken voters' ability to retain good politicians and punish opportunistic ones
Whether term limits can be welfare enhancing even when their direct effect is unambiguously negative, by interacting with other distortions in the political system
2727.scope: simple political agency model; the welfare gain comes from combining lower office value with better screening, and the direct effect of term limits alone is negative

2516.claim: Review: evidence on electoral punishment of corruption is mixed and often mild; information acquisition, blame attribution and behavioural response underlie a corruption-based vote, and a breakdown at any stage leaves corruption unpunished.

setting.unit_desc: review of studies across countries

identification.variation: survey of observational and experimental studies of voting responses to corruption

mechanisms.note: elections are assumed to curb corruption, but punishment can fail when information, blame attribution or behavioural response break down
blame attribution is one of the three stages whose failure explains weak punishment
audit disclosures hurt incumbents more where a local radio station disclosed the information

settled: Corruption harms society: lower tax revenues, investment and growth, equality, and well-being (Pani 2010; Mauro 1995; Chong & Calderon 2000; Tay et al. 2014)
Corruption erodes political trust and legitimacy (Della Porta 2000; Seligson 2002; Andersen & Tverdova 2003; Chang & Chu 2006)
Disclosed audit outcomes significantly affect incumbents' electoral performance, more so where a local radio station disclosed them
contested: Whether voters punish corruption at the ballot box: evidence is mixed and often suggests mild punishment, despite voters' general distaste for corruption

gaps: How voter coordination determines the extent to which corruption is punished at the ballot box
2516.scope: review of retrospective voting on corruption; punishment varies with information, partisanship and the economy

2753.claim: In South Indian village councils, elected councillors gain improved personal access to public resources and the head councillor's village and group are favoured; electoral incentives do not eliminate opportunism.

2753.outcome_desc: personal and household access to public resources (benefits) for councillors, and public good activism in the Pradhan's village

electoral incentives do not eliminate opportunism, though voters use electoral clout to gain access to resources
village elites cannot be the whole story because political institutions influence policy outcomes

contested: Whether local resource allocation is driven by village elites or by elected politicians' own interests and electoral clout (the Pradhan's village is favoured, but elites cannot be ruled out)
Whether electoral incentives curb politician opportunism: the paper finds they do not eliminate it
gaps: How far village elites shape local policy-making alongside political institutions, which these results cannot rule out
2753.data_asset: village-level and household survey data collected in 2002 in roughly 500 South Indian villages
2753.scope: South Indian Gram Panchayats under plurality rule; the Pradhan's-village effect is similar under direct and indirect election of the head councillor; disadvantaged groups gain when the head belongs to their group

2929.claim: Field experiments randomising candidate mailings find incumbent campaigns did not raise incumbent vote share while the challenger campaign was effective; incumbents maximising winning probability expect minimal vote-share gains.

Whether the original OLS finding of no vote return to incumbent spending was biased or merely misinterpreted, since incumbents may maximise winning probability rather than vote share
gaps: Experimental evidence on returns to incumbent and challenger spending, since observational research alone will likely fail to produce consensus
Tests of the further empirical predictions of the incumbent optimal-spending model, such as how returns vary with election competitiveness

2929.scope: campaign mailings in US partisan contests; incumbents' returns are minimal in vote share but may raise winning probability; returns vary with the competitiveness of the election

2873.claim: Edited NBER volume: the US now ranks among the least corrupt countries, but its clean reputation is modern; 19th- and early-20th-century American corruption resembled that of today's transition and developing economies.

International measures rank the United States today among the lowest 10 percent of countries worldwide in corruption

Whether partnerships were inferior: partnerships risked untimely dissolution, corporations dictatorial majority control, so each form had its own problem (Lamoreaux & Rosenthal)

2539.claim: The president's party is held accountable for county economic performance in nearly all local, state and federal elections (1969-2018); incumbents are also held accountable for the economy in US House elections.
2539.treatment_desc: change in local (county) economic conditions, measured by administrative wage data, interacted with the party of the president, governor or incumbent

1218.claim: In non-democracies without commitment, a ruling coalition must be powerful enough and self-enforcing (no subcoalition able to secede and rule); such coalitions always exist and are generically unique, and axiomatic and game approaches coincide.
1218.treatment_desc: absence of institutions enabling political commitment, with individuals endowed with political power (model)
1218.outcome_desc: identity and size of the ruling coalition; distribution of resources

setting.unit_desc: theoretical society of individuals with heterogeneous political power

identification.variation: axiomatic approach and a dynamic coalition-formation game whose subgame-perfect equilibria coincide with the axiomatic ruling coalitions

mechanisms.note: members cannot commit to distributions or to not sidelining fellow members, so coalitions must be self-enforcing
ruling coalition is self-enforcing only if no sufficiently powerful subcoalition can secede

settled: Commitment problems in political decision making are pervasive where institutions are weak (Acemoglu Robinson 2006; weakly institutionalized polities, Acemoglu Robinson Verdier 2004)
gaps: Extending coalition formation to games played repeatedly and subject to shocks
Relaxing the assumption that sidelined individuals have no say in future decision making
Applying the framework to more concrete problems
1218.scope: existence and uniqueness are generic results for general societies; no empirical application

2057.claim: A randomized property-tax campaign in Kananga, DRC raised tax compliance from 0.1% to 11.6% and raised political participation by about 5 percentage points (31%), consistent with a participation dividend from tax bargaining.
2057.treatment_desc: randomized door-to-door property tax registration and collection campaign, the first of its kind in the city
2057.outcome_desc: attending town hall meetings and submitting government evaluations; beliefs about the provincial government

magnitudes.outcome: property tax compliance (control 0.1%, treatment 11.6%)
political participation (town hall attendance / government evaluation)
political participation, relative increase

setting.unit_desc: neighborhoods of Kananga randomized into the tax campaign

identification.variation: random assignment of the tax campaign across neighborhoods; surveys at baseline, midline and endline
identification.threat: spillovers to control neighborhoods (estimated using random variation in adjacent treated neighborhoods) and informational effects of learning about the campaign

mechanisms.note: some evidence that the campaign signalled state capacity and raised the expected benefits of participation; evidence on bargaining channel is suggestive

settled: The ability to tax is central to state capacity and development (Kaldor 1963; Besley and Persson 2013)
contested: Whether taxation catalyses political participation and accountable governance through tax bargaining in fragile states (Schumpeter 1918; Tilly 1985 for early modern Europe)
gaps: How the government responds to tax-induced participation, e.g. with public goods (beyond the scope; public goods provided at a more aggregated unit than the randomization unit)
Mechanisms behind the participation response are only suggestive (bargaining for public goods and inclusive governance vs. state-capacity signal)
2057.data_asset: field experiment with baseline, midline and endline surveys and administrative tax payments
2057.scope: fragile-state setting where most citizens had never been registered or taxed; participation rises for all solicited households, not only those who pay

1377.claim: The Great Plains buffalo slaughter was triggered by a European tanning innovation and sustained by foreign demand for hides, acting through very elastic demand and open access to hunting rather than the usual suspects.
1377.treatment_desc: tanning innovation making buffalo hides valuable industrial leather, with fixed world prices and European demand
1377.outcome_desc: buffalo kill, hunter entry and herd size on the Great Plains

setting.unit_desc: Great Plains buffalo herd; hide export and import-share statistics from several countries

identification.variation: timing of the tanning innovation and US-specific shares of European hide imports, combined with a dynamic open-access model and first-person accounts
identification.threat: evidence is largely circumstantial

settled: Hide hunting, the US Army, native overhunting and the railroads are typically held responsible for the slaughter
contested: Whether international trade, rather than the usual suspects, drove the slaughter (role of trade featured minimally in prior accounts)
gaps: The Canadian case of bison extinction is left for future work
1377.data_asset: constructed hide export data from international trade statistics, plus diaries and newspaper accounts
1377.scope: explains the punctuated slaughter on the plains after 1872; requires very elastic demand, open access and a new tanning process jointly

952.claim: When the strong party controls a source of unrest, it wins more often the less is known about its ability to cause unrest, because a better-informed weak party can moderate to a centrist platform; uncertainty over the threat's credibility leads to platform div
952.treatment_desc: a party able to instigate political unrest (riots, strikes, coups) if it loses the election (model)
952.outcome_desc: platform choice, which party wins, and implemented policy

setting.unit_desc: theoretical two-party majority-rule election with a one-dimensional policy space; illustrated with UK, Taiwan, El Salvador and Liberia

identification.variation: model comparing platform commitment vs. none, and public vs. private information about the strong party's ability to cause unrest

mechanisms.note: the strong party becomes more likely to win as voter fear of disruption grows when the risk of unrest is its private information
signalling by the strong party under private information produces platform divergence
platform convergence arises with commitment and no private information, but the strong party wins on the convergent policy if it controls a serious threat

gaps: Elections with more than two parties or more than one threatening actor (model has two parties and a single threatening actor; the convergence theorem fails with more than two parties, Shepsle 1991)
952.scope: results depend on whether the threat is controlled by the strong party or by an outsider, and on whether risk is privately known; robust to large benefits of office only when an outsider controls the threat

1387.claim: Italian municipal governments headed by women are more likely to end early (female mayors have an early-resignation probability 17% to 54% higher than men), especially with all-male councils and in regions with less favourable attitudes to working women.
1387.treatment_desc: mayor being a woman (including close mixed-gender races)
1387.outcome_desc: early termination of the municipal legislature (government stability)

magnitudes.outcome: probability of early termination, female vs male mayor (lower end of range)
probability of early termination, female vs male mayor (upper end of range)
probability of early termination, RD local linear, mixed-gender races
probability of early termination, RD local linear, narrower sample

setting.unit_desc: universe of Italian municipal governments elected 1993-2003

identification.variation: narrow margins in gender-mixed mayoral races, alongside municipality fixed effects in the full sample
identification.threat: non-random sorting of women into municipalities and types of races (women less likely to run where governing is difficult)

mechanisms.note: leader gender matters for outcomes; effect strongest with all-male councils, pointing to male councillors resisting a woman's lead

settled: Women remain underrepresented in leadership positions in business, academia and government (Bertrand and Hallock 2001)
gaps: How women fare once they reach the top of an organization is little known
Whether group dynamics found in Italian councils extend to other hierarchies such as corporate boards and CEOs, and to other countries
1387.data_asset: universe of Italian municipal governments elected 1993-2003 with duration of legislature
1387.scope: concentrated where the council is entirely male and in regions with less favourable attitudes toward working women; authors expect relevance for similar-culture countries (France, UK)

ev.intro: These papers were read from the PDF itself, not just the abstract, and coded the same way: what varies, what is measured, which way the effect goes, how large, where, with what design, and which canonical model it speaks to. That makes papers comparable, and comparable papers make a map. A causal question here is one cause crossed with one outcome — information to voters against turnout, quotas against spending. The matrix below is the field's answer sheet: where the signs line up, where they split, and the large empty areas where nobody has asked. Every paper in the atlas with a readable PDF has been read this way; a thin cell therefore means the question is little studied rather than little read. Each paper's drawer says how it was read and how confident the coding is.
ev.contestedIntro: Questions where papers measuring the same thing reach opposite answers — and the list is short on purpose. Finding them takes two stages. First an automatic test: a pair counts only when one paper finds an increase and another a decrease or no effect, and their descriptions of what they measured overlap, so a turnout study is never counted against a vote-share study. That test alone proposed 26 candidates. Reading them paper by paper kept 7. Thirteen were not one question at all (‘information to voters’ bundles turnout drives, corruption disclosures and persuasion experiments), and six were the same finding framed from opposite ends — ‘mayors eligible for re-election steal less’ and ‘second-term mayors steal more’ carry opposite signs and agree completely. What survives is worth your attention precisely because three quarters of the candidates did not: each one is a contribution defined before the work starts, a design that discriminates between the camps in a setting that breaks the tie.
ev.gapsIntro: This page reads the literature for what it has not done. The panel below gathers every opening into one ranked list; the sections after it are the raw material, each a different kind of absence. What the authors say is missing is the field's own words, taken from ~2,500 open questions written in their conclusions and grouped so you can see which ones recur. A hole is a cause and an outcome both well measured that nobody has crossed, with the conceptual non-starters removed by hand. A claim that has not travelled rests on a single country. A design monoculture inherits one strategy's blind spot. And a question the frontier left behind may have been settled on data since superseded. Nothing here is a verdict on what is worth doing — it is where the evidence stops.

F1.claim: Politicians favour visible, attributable benefits over quality
F1.detail: Cash transfers, roads and electrification are politically legible; learning, clinical quality and maintenance are not, so incumbents over-invest in the first.

F2.claim: Voters punish malfeasance more reliably than they reward delivery
F2.detail: Audits revealing corruption cost votes; better schools or clinics are rewarded inconsistently, so reforms rarely become self-sustaining.

F3.claim: Who governs matters as much as the rules
F3.detail: Reserved seats for women, castes and tribes shift provision toward their priorities; pay, recruitment and training reshape politician quality.

F4.claim: Reducing material dependence weakens clientelism more than information
F4.detail: Cisterns and cash transfers free voters to act on preferences; informed but vulnerable voters can be bought back.

F5.detail: Unions, patronage networks and local elites are concentrated and mobilised; future beneficiaries are diffuse. Good reforms get weakened, delayed or reversed.

F6.claim: Bureaucratic quality mediates whether political will becomes delivery
F6.detail: Personnel rules, credentials and oversight bodies can stop managers from directing frontline workers; political will and capacity are complements.

agenda.title: Your agenda: socially beneficial reform
agenda.intro: Your research brief asks why democracies that can produce evidence about problems fail to turn it into policy, especially policies with diffuse, delayed, hard-to-attribute benefits. This view lays the atlas along the causal chain in the brief and along its four failure types, so you can see which links the literature has covered with credible evidence and where the frontier is thin.

links.name: Evidence → public knowledge
links.text: Does evidence reach citizens? Media coverage, report cards and disclosures move what voters know; coverage follows audiences and owners.

links.name: Knowledge → perceived problem
links.text: Information is framed, slanted and filtered. Persuasion, propaganda and social media decide whether knowledge becomes a perceived problem.

links.name: Perceived problem → policy preference
links.text: Beliefs about fairness, mobility, identity and economic insecurity shape whether a recognised problem becomes support for a policy.

links.name: Preference → collective organisation
links.text: The Olson problem: diffuse beneficiaries rarely organise, while concentrated losers do. Protest and movements are the main counter-technology.

links.name: Organisation → political salience
links.text: Movements, lobbies and news cycles decide what politicians attend to; salience is crowded out by other events.

links.name: Salience → electoral accountability
links.text: Accountability needs observability, attribution, salience and a short feedback loop; the evidence shows punishment works better than reward.

links.name: Accountability → legislative adoption
links.text: Bargaining, agenda power, parties and money decide which salient demands become law.

links.name: Adoption → bureaucratic implementation
links.text: Laws pass through bureaucracies whose selection, incentives, autonomy and oversight decide whether they are implemented.

links.name: Implementation → observable outcome
links.text: Frontline effort, leakage and local capture separate implemented policy from realised outcomes.

links.name: Outcome → electoral feedback
links.text: Whether visible results are credited to the right politician closes the loop — or doesn't, for diffuse and delayed benefits.

links.name: Feedback → reform survival
links.text: Reforms that leave organised losers intact are reversed; surviving reforms change the political equilibrium.

failures.name: Preference failure
failures.text: People do not want the policy, because of values or its distributional effects.
failures.open: Which features of a diffuse-benefit policy (framing, who pays, identity cues) move preferences durably rather than for one survey round?

failures.name: Information failure
failures.text: People want it but do not know it is beneficial or who delivered it.
failures.open: How does attribution fail when several tiers share a service, and what replaces local news as it declines?

failures.name: Political-aggregation failure
failures.text: People want it, but small organised groups block it.
failures.open: What lets diffuse beneficiaries become a political actor — organisations, outsiders, or policy design that creates its own constituency?

failures.name: Implementation failure
failures.text: It is legislated but not implemented, because of bureaucracy, capacity or vested interests.
failures.open: Which bureaucratic reforms are politically feasible, and how do oversight bodies avoid becoming their own bottleneck?

dlTiers.4: abstract only, taught in 3+ courses: the introduction would sharpen design and mechanism coding

meta.lede: A map of the political-economy literature as top PhD programmes teach it in 2026: every paper on ~90 syllabi and lecture decks, deduplicated, placed on one tree, linked by citations, and read against the canonical models it tests. The VoxDevLit review on public service delivery is the anchor.
meta.thesis: Across the syllabi, the field has moved from cross-country correlations about institutions to micro-evidence on the agents inside them: voters with limited information, politicians selected and disciplined by elections, brokers and bureaucrats who sit between policy and delivery. The 2015-onward readings concentrate on four fronts: accountability with imperfect information (punishment works better than reward; visibility beats quality), who governs (selection and representation), the state's own agents (bureaucratic selection, incentives and autonomy) and information ecosystems (social media, polarisation, autocratic control). Older canon on institutions, conflict and redistribution theory remains, but its share of new readings is falling. Read against the canonical models, the median-voter account of redistribution is the most contested: over two in five of its tests qualify or contradict it, while models of bureaucratic incentives, media influence and lobbying are almost uniformly supported.
meta.mechIntro: Patrick Francois's BREAD lecture lists the recurring strategic architectures of political economy — voters disciplining politicians, citizens deciding to run, promises that cannot be made credible, groups spending resources to win. Each mechanism below starts from its canonical model and its predictions, then lists every coded paper that tests it, with my reading of whether the evidence supports the prediction, qualifies it (the effect depends on conditions the model treats as fixed), or contradicts it.
meta.netIntro: Edges come from the reference lists of papers resolved in OpenAlex: a link means the newer paper cites the older one and both are in the atlas. Filled dots are syllabus papers; hollow rings are works no syllabus lists but that at least ten syllabus papers cite, added by following the reference lists one step out. Colour is the branch family; size grows with the number of courses assigning the paper and how often other atlas papers build on it.
meta.mtreeIntro: The canonical mechanisms of political economy as a tree. Each architecture branches into its mechanisms; each mechanism into the models that state it and the empirical papers that test it, split by verdict — supports, qualifies (the effect depends on conditions the model treats as fixed) or contradicts. Open a mechanism to see who tested it, when, where and with what design.
meta.authIntro: Every author of an atlas paper resolved in OpenAlex, placed at their current institution (OpenAlex's last known affiliation, which can lag recent moves). The left chart shows whether the field's centre of gravity is shifting; the map and ranking show where the centres are; the network shows who writes with whom. Authors of papers OpenAlex could not resolve (mostly books and working papers) are missing.
meta.mapIntro: Country of study for empirical papers, coded from my reading of the review, abstracts and titles. The United States accounts for about a third of single-country studies; among developing countries India, Brazil, China and Indonesia lead because of audit lotteries, close elections, reservations and administrative data. Whole regions with weak data remain nearly blank. Cross-country and theory papers are not on the map.
meta.revIntro: Pick what you care about and the atlas assembles a structured review from its own codings: the scope of the evidence, an answer section for each of your questions, the foundations and frontier of each topic, the mechanisms tested and how often the evidence supports them, gaps, and references. It does not write prose. For a narrative review, copy the prompt: it bundles this outline with every selected paper's coded record, so Claude or ChatGPT writes from the evidence rather than from memory. Your choices are remembered in this browser.
meta.timeIntro: Three views of time. The first shows when the assigned papers were published, so you can see which waves of work the syllabi lean on. The map below it shows where that evidence was produced, year by year. The last follows each canonical mechanism from its model to the empirical tests that came later.
meta.courseIntro: Each course is a different cut of the same field. MIT's 14.773 leans on institutions, conflict and history; the BREAD-IGC and PUC-Rio courses on accountability, selection and bureaucracy; Stockholm and Harvard on elections, legislatures and media; Chicago's 2026 courses on culture and context. The matrix makes those choices comparable.
meta.dlNote: Papers whose introduction I could not read, in four tiers. Tiers 1–3 I could place only from the title and syllabus context; tier 4 I coded from the abstract alone, and the introduction would sharpen the design and mechanism verdicts. Open copies were blocked for my scripts (publisher and SSRN pages refuse automated downloads) but usually open in your browser or through your library login. The same list, with every link, is in download_list.csv
meta.foot: Built 2026-10-27 from 132 syllabi, reading lists and lecture decks in 3.research_statement/input. Metadata from Crossref and OpenAlex; citation links from OpenAlex reference lists. Classification into the tree is mine, reviewed title by title; findings and mechanism verdicts are my reading of the VoxDevLit review, abstracts and introductions, flagged per paper. 1494 papers were read from the PDF itself — abstract, introduction, results, conclusion, table captions and the authors' own statements about what is settled, contested and open — and the evidence matrix, the contested questions and the gap map are built from that read alone. Each paper's drawer says which level it was read at and how confident the coding is. Treat verdicts as a reader's map, not a meta-analysis. 360 political-economy works no syllabus lists were added by following reference lists one step out (each cited by at least ten syllabus papers; hollow nodes, marked “ref”). Authors' current institutions come from OpenAlex, scored by the institutions on their own recent papers and affiliation history; disambiguation errors remain possible.
